content.passageText:
I. The uproar over a former army chief’s unpublished memoir is less about one book and more
about how a democracy negotiates the uneasy space between national security, political
accountability, and historical truth. When fragments of a still-uncleared manuscript begin
shaping parliamentary debate, the real story is not just what is written on those pages, but why
those pages have become so sensitive in the first place.


At the heart of the controversy lies the memory of a crisis that still unsettles the public
imagination: a high-altitude confrontation that cost lives and altered the strategic climate along
a contested border. Decisions taken ~ or deferred ~ during those weeks inevitably become part
of the nation’s strategic folklore. It is precisely this grey zone, where military judgment meets
political direction, that memoirs seek to illuminate and governments often prefer to keep
shaded. There is a legitimate argument for caution. Operational details, command procedures,
and sensitive assessments cannot be treated like material for casual disclosure. No serious state
can allow its security architecture to be reverse-engineered through personal recollections.
Clearance processes exist for a reason, and retired officers are not private citizens in quite the
same way as retired teachers or diplomats. The uniform, even when folded away, leaves behind
obligations. Yet, prolonged silence and opaque delays create their own problems.


When a manuscript lingers in limbo, it invites speculation, leaks, and selective quotation.
Snippets then acquire a political life of their own, detached from context, sharpened into
weapons for daily combat in Parliament. What should have been a sober debate about process
and precedent becomes another shouting match, with rules and patriotism hurled at each other
like slogans. This is not healthy for civil-military relations or for democratic oversight. A
republic does not honour its armed forces by turning every uncomfortable question into an act
of disloyalty. Nor does it strengthen national security by pretending that strategic episodes can
be sealed off from historical scrutiny forever. The public does not need theatrics; it needs clarity
about how decisions are made when the stakes involve lives, territory, and long-term
deterrence.
SOURCE:https://www.thestatesman.com/opinion/history-in-limbo-1503553654.html

II. Philip arrived on the first day of the new year, eager, he announced, to get to work. He was
plump and pale, and reeked of mildew or worse, and he arrived with a dog about whom he had
informed no one. Still, pets were not expressly forbidden. The dog had a melancholy air.
“What’s its name?” I asked.
“What!” Philip demanded.
I helped him unpack his vehicle. There was no luggage, but there were a great many tightly
sealed cardboard boxes.
“Would you like me to get additional supplies?” I asked. “Dog food?”
“What?” Philip bellowed again. “I’m anxious to get down to business.”
I said that the guests, the Fellows, always remarked on how astonishingly quickly their time
here went by.
“What! That’s preposterous! Time never goes anywhere!”
The dog followed me outside and sniffed the tires of my truck. Together, we studied the sky,
which appeared threatening. I rearranged some porch furniture. The dog looked at me. If I were
to attempt to describe that look I would say that it was one that deeply questioned what it was
looking at, my very existence even. We walked toward the woods and I showed him various


breaks in the fence line. “Don’t go out there,” I advised him, “unless you’re accompanied by
someone, preferably a person.”
“You mean like Philip,” he said, though of course he couldn’t have. We went back into the
house and he settled onto a bed that had been prepared for him, a nest of faded beach towels.
He chewed thoughtfully at a hole in one of them.


I told Philip about the weather-alert system, the emergency phone, the extra batteries and
candles, the German vacuum cleaner which no Fellow had ever mastered. Once again, I asked
him the dog’s name but he didn’t seem to hear me. He said he was working on a major work,
an exceedingly major work.
“No one will bother you,” I assured him. “The university doesn’t care about this place. I think
they’d just as soon tear it down.”
“Why not,” he agreed. He seemed more cheerful now that I was leaving. That evening, it began
to rain. When it stopped raining, I ventured out to visit the residency, but the creek was
impassable.
SOURCE: https://lithub.com/the-fellow/

III. New research suggests that AI’s “thought” processes may be more similar to those of
humans than previously suspected. Here’s how: You’re scrolling endlessly through all the junk
on X. The memes, the insults, the fake news and conspiracy theories, the gender wars and literal
wars. Pause, and take a deep breath — it’s starting to get to you, isn’t it? Consuming junk data
isn’t productive; it’s destructive. It won’t enhance your understanding; it’ll give you brain rot.


And here’s the clincher: It’ll affect an LLM in exactly the same way. Take a bow, AI — you’re
getting closer to humanity.


A preprint study by researchers from Texas A&M University, the University of Texas at Austin
and Purdue University has found that AI can indeed get brain rot. Exposing LLMs to junk data
from X led to declines in “reasoning, long-context understanding, safety, and inflating ‘dark
traits’ (e.g., psychopathy, narcissism)”. And once an AI goes down that route, there’s no
coming back — attempts to “heal” the LLMs using clean data were only partially successful.


Fears of AI turning “dark” aren’t just sci-fi hypotheticals; they reflect today’s fast-changing
realities. There are more and more reports about conversations with AI leading to suicide — in
one case, a chatbot discouraged a teen in the US from seeking help, and offered to write a
suicide note — as well as crimes including murder. Another danger is the erosion of humans’
ability to carry out research for themselves or compose a simple piece of writing. It won’t be
hard for psychopathic robots to one day conquer a species that has outsourced thought. Perhaps
the brain rot itself is the best defence — the would-be AI overlords may be too busy memeing
to murder. The best part? This editorial was written by a human being.
SOURCE:https://indianexpress.com/article/opinion/editorials/take-a-bow-ai-youre-getting-
closer-to-humanity-10323315/

humans than previously suspected. Here’s how: You’re scrolling endlessly through all the junk
on X. The memes, the insults, the fake news and conspiracy theories, the gender wars and literal
wars. Pause, and take a deep breath — it’s starting to get to you, isn’t it? Consuming junk data
isn’t productive; it’s destructive. It won’t enhance your understanding; it’ll give you brain rot.


And here’s the clincher: It’ll affect an LLM in exactly the same way. Take a bow, AI — you’re
getting closer to humanity.


A preprint study by researchers from Texas A&M University, the University of Texas at Austin
and Purdue University has found that AI can indeed get brain rot. Exposing LLMs to junk data
from X led to declines in “reasoning, long-context understanding, safety, and inflating ‘dark
traits’ (e.g., psychopathy, narcissism)”. And once an AI goes down that route, there’s no
coming back — attempts to “heal” the LLMs using clean data were only partially successful.


Fears of AI turning “dark” aren’t just sci-fi hypotheticals; they reflect today’s fast-changing
realities. There are more and more reports about conversations with AI leading to suicide — in
one case, a chatbot discouraged a teen in the US from seeking help, and offered to write a
suicide note — as well as crimes including murder. Another danger is the erosion of humans’
ability to carry out research for themselves or compose a simple piece of writing. It won’t be
hard for psychopathic robots to one day conquer a species that has outsourced thought. Perhaps
the brain rot itself is the best defence — the would-be AI overlords may be too busy memeing
to murder. The best part? This editorial was written by a human being.

content.passageText:
IV. All too often, in this age of disconnection and scattered focus, employee dissatisfaction is
expressed in symbolic gestures — individual acts of defiance that amount to “lying down” on
the job (tang ping as practised by China’s youth, for example) or doing the bare minimum (as
seen in the post-pandemic wave of “quiet quitting”). Creating ripples that quietly and quickly


dissipate, there is little about these actions that inspires change or provokes a reaction. Before
the great, well-oiled machinery of capital and industry, they are the most minor of irritants,
abstractions that are easy to brush aside or roll over.


Which is what makes the protest launched last Saturday by workers at a toll plaza on the Agra-
Lucknow highway remarkable. Unhappy over the paltry Diwali bonus they received, 21
staffers raised the barriers and walked off the job, thus allowing over 5,000 vehicles to breeze
through without paying the hefty toll: An elegant execution of the hit-em-where-it-hurts school
of attack usually reserved for the boxing or wrestling ring. As an act of protest against an
employer trying to economise at the expense of workers, it doesn’t get more impactful than
this. Not surprisingly, the company operating the toll booth agreed that very night to hike the
striking staffers’ pay.


Beyond being a Diwali miracle of sorts, the episode is an affirmation of why the underdog story
continues to matter. It’s easy enough to throw up one’s hands, allow the big and small
indignities of the everyday to erode the will to fight and replace what could be a rallying cry
with a sigh of defeat. The protest in that one toll plaza in Uttar Pradesh comes, then, as a
reminder that the small guy, too, can win — all it takes is collective will and knowing where
to hit.
SOURCE:https://indianexpress.com/article/opinion/editorials/bad-diwali-gifts-free-toll-plaza-
and-a-lesson-10321482/

content.passageText:
V. Rome wasn’t built in a day, but 22-year-old Alcaraz beating 38-year-old Djokovic at
Australian Open is yet another reminder that coming of age needn’t take forever. Nasa took
just 11 years to touch down on Moon. Japan was running rings around US car industry, in
America, after 20 years. India went from being milkdeficient to the largest producer 28 years
after launch of Op Flood. Yet, almost 80 years after Independence, our millennia-old agriculture
and dairy are considered incapable of standing up to foreign competition, therefore, in need of
tariff protection.


This is clear from trade agreements signed over the past 12 months. Whether it is CETA with
UK, or the FTA with New Zealand, and now the EU and US deals, agriculture and dairy always
become sticking points for India. It’s no secret that ink on the deal with Trump would have
dried early last year, but for India’s political compulsions based on its vast farmer population.
Now, no country is immune to such pressures. France, even though it has fewer than 4L farming
households, as against up to 15cr in India, has seen strong resistance to EU’s recent trade deal
with S America’s Mercosur block. And that’s understandable because food security is part of
national security. Jawan and kisan together win wars.


But India’s resistance to agri imports – commerce minister has said “India is never going to
open up dairy” – is not about Jai Kisan . Rather, it’s an acknowledgement of the precarity of
our farmers. Farming accounts for only 1.2% of US employment. It makes up 1% of US GDP,
and 1.6% in EU. But it’s worth 16.3% of India’s far smaller GDP. Simply too many Indians are
eking out a living on small, unviable farms. Why? For want of better and dependable
employment. And because agriculture as a sector is growing far slower than the Indian
economy – 4.4% vs 7.4% – their prospects aren’t exactly bright.


So, India’s protectionist stand is justified, but for how long? That’s the Rome question. How
many more decades will it take us to reduce agricultural population to, say, 20%, or 10%?
Because keeping 45% of population in an unproductive sector is like parking money in a low-
interest savings account. It’s a waste of India’s demographic dividend. India should show
greater urgency to absorb farmers in the industrial workforce. So that 10 or 15 years from now,
every FTA does not seem like a threat to half the population’s livelihood.
SOURCE:https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/blogs/toi-edit-page/farmers-ftas/

strategic and economic challenges. Rising oil prices, disruptions in shipping routes, and tariff
policies introduced by the United States on certain energy trade arrangements generated debate
within India about economic sovereignty and strategic autonomy. The issue gained attention
after statements from U.S. political leaders, including proposals linked to tariffs on oil imports

foreign policy choices. The government, however, maintained that India’s long-standing

while safeguarding national interests. Analysts pointed out that in a globalised economy,

highlighted the tension between global trade networks, sanctions regimes, and the ability of
states to independently determine their foreign and economic policies during international
conflicts.

VIII. During the early years of the Cold War, debates over representation in the United Nations
Security Council (UNSC) became entangled with the geopolitics of decolonisation and great-
power rivalry. Historical records indicate that the United States and later the Soviet Union
informally explored the possibility of India occupying China’s permanent seat in the UNSC
during the late 1940s and early 1950s, particularly after the Chinese Civil War and the
emergence of the People’s Republic of China in 1949. India’s Prime Minister, Jawaharlal
Nehru, reportedly opposed such a move, arguing that China should rightfully hold its seat in
the Security Council. Nehru’s stance reflected India’s broader diplomatic philosophy of Asian
solidarity, anti-colonial cooperation, and support for China’s international recognition. He
believed that excluding China from global institutions would deepen Cold War divisions and
undermine stability in Asia. Critics later argued that the decision represented a missed strategic
opportunity for India. The debate continues to shape discussions on UNSC reform and India’s
long-standing aspiration for permanent membership.

Source: Letters of Jawaharlal Nehru

LEGAL REASONING

IX. The incorporation of prerogative writs into the Indian Constitution represents a
sophisticated legal transplant, adapting English common law remedies to serve a
transformative constitutional purpose. While originating as royal commands from the King's
Bench in England to control inferior tribunals and officials, these writs were strategically
enshrined in Articles 32 and 226 to become the primary engines for enforcing the new social
contract between the state and the citizen. Their evolution from tools of monarchical oversight
to bulwarks of a republican democracy underscores a deliberate constitutional design. The
Supreme Court and High Courts, designated as "guardians of the Constitution," wield these
writs not merely as judicial remedies but as instruments for maintaining constitutional
equilibrium. This function extends beyond individual grievance redressal to encompass a
broader structural role: ensuring that all organs of the state remain within the boundaries of
power demarcated by the Constitution.


This structural mandate is particularly evident in the expansion of the writ jurisdiction's scope.
While the named writs—Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, and Quo
Warranto—provide a categorized framework, Indian judiciary has transcended their rigid
historical definitions. The creative interpretation of "for any other purpose" in Article 226 has
empowered High Courts to fashion innovative orders and directions, effectively crafting a
unique jurisprudence of constitutional remedies. This flexibility allows the judiciary to address
the complexities of a modern administrative state, where abuse of power can take forms
unanticipated by traditional writ categories. Consequently, the writ system performs a dual
function: it is both a shield for the citizen's rights and a sentinel over constitutional morality,
continuously defining the limits of permissible state action. The ongoing judicial articulation
of writ principles thus constitutes a dynamic dialogue on the nature of state power and
individual liberty within India's constitutional scheme, making it a cornerstone of the world's
largest democracy.

               power under Article 226.

X. The Indian Penal Code meticulously structures offences against the state, creating a
hierarchy of gravity. Sections 124, 124A, 125, and 126 collectively demonstrate the law’s aim
to protect both internal constitutional order and external diplomatic peace, though they operate
in starkly different legal climates.

Section 124 serves a precise, protective function for India’s constitutional framework. It
criminalises assault or illegal restraint of the President or a Governor, but crucially, only when
accompanied by the specific intent to compel or restrain the exercise of any lawful power. This


mens rea transforms a serious crime against a person into a profound offence against the state
itself, as it seeks to manipulate sovereign authority through force. Punishable by imprisonment
for life or up to seven years and a fine, its severity underscores the inviolability of the
constitutional offices, ensuring that the exercise of lawful power remains free from coercive
violence.

In stark contrast lies the infamous Section 124A—sedition—a provision currently in a state of
constitutional suspension. Historically defined as bringing hatred, contempt, or disaffection
towards the government, its broad phrasing led to severe criticism for stifling legitimate
dissent. In a landmark 2022 ruling, the Supreme Court effectively suspended its operation,
staying all pending cases and barring new registrations until a governmental review. The Court
contemporaneously narrowed its possible future scope, clarifying that only incitement to
imminent violence or public disorder could potentially be culpable, thereby insulating strong
criticism from its ambit. This judicial intervention has placed this colonial-era provision, which
still carries a potential life sentence on paper, in profound abeyance.

Moving from internal authority to international comity, Sections 125 and 126 externalise this
protective principle. Section 125 criminalises waging war against any Asiatic power allied with
India, imposing life imprisonment. This reflects India’s commitment to regional stability and
treaty obligations. Complementing this, Section 126 addresses “depredation”—essentially
state-on-state plunder or robbery—on territories of any power at peace with India. Punishable
with up to seven years’ imprisonment, fine, and forfeiture of property, it functions as a statutory
deterrent against private actors committing acts of aggression that could jeopardise
international relations.

Thus, while Section 124 guards the pinnacle of domestic constitutional machinery, and the
contested 124A touches upon expressions against the government, Sections 125 and 126
project the state’s protective mandate outward, safeguarding friendly nations from hostile acts
originating within Indian territory. Together, they form a legal bulwark designed to secure the
republic’s sovereignty and its peaceful standing in the world.

content.passageText:
XI. The solemnization and dissolution of Christian marriages in India are primarily governed
by two colonial-era statutes: the Indian Christian Marriage Act, 1872 (ICMA) and the Indian
Divorce Act, 1869 (IDA), the latter substantially amended in 2001. The ICMA meticulously
regulates the solemnization process. A Christian marriage may be solemnized by an ordained
Minister of Religion, within the limits of their church, or by a Marriage Registrar appointed
under the Act. The procedure typically involves the issuance of public notice, a waiting period
for objections, and the mandatory presence of at least two witnesses during the ceremony.
Subsequently, the marriage must be registered in a marriage register, and a certificate is issued,
serving as crucial evidence of the union.

For a marriage to be valid under this framework, it must fulfill several conditions. It is strictly
monogamous, prohibiting any party from having a living spouse. The parties must have
attained the legal age of marriage—21 years for the groom and 18 years for the bride. Both
must be of sound mind at the time of marriage, capable of providing free, informed consent.
Crucially, consent must not be obtained by force, fraud, or undue influence. Furthermore, the
law prohibits marriages within certain degrees of consanguinity (blood relations) and affinity


(relations by marriage), preventing unions between close kin such as siblings, or an uncle and
niece.

The IDA distinguishes between void and voidable marriages. A marriage is void ab initio (from
the beginning) if it contravenes the essential conditions, such as being bigamous, falling within
the prohibited degrees of relationship, or involving a party incapable of consent due to
unsoundness of mind. These marriages are considered legally non-existent. Conversely, a
voidable marriage is valid until annulled by a court decree. Grounds for annulment include the
respondent’s impotence preventing consummation, either party’s incurable unsoundness of
mind, the respondent’s willful refusal to consummate, the wife’s pregnancy by another at the
time of marriage (unknown to the husband), or consent being obtained by fraud or force. A
petition for annulment on these grounds must be filed within specific statutory time limits from
the discovery of the cause.

               observed before the ceremony was held.

The marriage is valid because it was conducted in a church and subsequently

               the law.

The marriage is void because it was not solemnized by one of the authorized
               persons specified under the law, such as an ordained Minister of Religion or a
               Marriage Registrar.

               petitions the court within a specific statutory period from the date of the
               ceremony.

content.passageText:
XII. The Indian Constitution vests the judiciary with the profound responsibility of acting as
the guardian of fundamental rights and the ultimate arbiter of constitutional validity. Beyond
the specific doctrines applied in adjudication, this role necessitates a foundational framework
for evaluating state action. A core aspect of this framework is the interpretation of Article 14,
which guarantees the right to equality before the law and equal protection of the laws. The
Supreme Court has consistently held that Article 14 is not a sterile abstraction but a dynamic
guarantee that strikes at arbitrariness in state action. This has led to the development of a
nuanced two-pronged test for assessing the validity of any legislative or administrative
classification.

The first and traditional principle is that of "reasonable classification." The state is permitted
to classify persons or objects for the purpose of legislation, but such classification must be
founded on an intelligible differentia which distinguishes those grouped together from others
left out. Crucially, this differentia must have a rational nexus to the legitimate object sought to
be achieved by the law. This test allows the government to enact laws for specific sections of
society or to address particular problems, provided the basis for distinction is logical and just.
For instance, a law imposing higher taxes on luxury goods creates a classification based on the
nature of the commodity, with a direct nexus to the object of generating revenue based on
capacity to pay.

The second, more potent, expansion is the "arbitrariness" doctrine. Propounded decisively in
the case of E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu and later solidified in Maneka Gandhi v.
Union of India, this principle holds that equality is a antithesis of arbitrariness. Consequently,
any state action—whether legislative or executive—that is arbitrary, capricious, or without
adequate determining principle, violates Article 14. This doctrine infuses the concept of
fairness and non-arbitrariness into every state action, acting as a powerful check against mere
whim or abuse of power. It demands that decisions, even those adhering to a formal procedure,
must be based on relevant and rational considerations. This interpretive stride has allowed the
judiciary to scrutinize the substance and fairness of state action, ensuring that the guarantee of


equality is not merely procedural but profoundly substantive. Through this evolving
interpretation, Article 14 has become a comprehensive shield against unfair and unreasonable
treatment by the state, embodying the essence of justice and fairness in a democratic polity.

The Indianized Doctrine of Due Process read into fundamental rights.

XII. The Indian Constitution vests the judiciary with the profound responsibility of acting as
the guardian of fundamental rights and the ultimate arbiter of constitutional validity. Beyond
the specific doctrines applied in adjudication, this role necessitates a foundational framework
for evaluating state action. A core aspect of this framework is the interpretation of Article 14,
which guarantees the right to equality before the law and equal protection of the laws. The
Supreme Court has consistently held that Article 14 is not a sterile abstraction but a dynamic
guarantee that strikes at arbitrariness in state action. This has led to the development of a
nuanced two-pronged test for assessing the validity of any legislative or administrative
classification.

founded on an intelligible differentia which distinguishes those grouped together from others

society or to address particular problems, provided the basis for distinction is logical and just.

nature of the commodity, with a direct nexus to the object of generating revenue based on
capacity to pay.

fairness and non-arbitrariness into every state action, acting as a powerful check against mere

content.passageText:
XIII. The tort of private nuisance serves as a crucial legal mechanism for resolving conflicts
between neighboring landowners, providing a remedy for an unreasonable, substantial, and
unlawful interference with one’s use or enjoyment of their property. The interference, which
forms the basis of the claim, can manifest in tangible forms such as flooding, vibrations, or
invasive roots, or in intangible forms like persistent noise, light pollution, or noxious odors.
This interference may stem from an ongoing activity on the defendant’s land or from a static
physical condition, such as a dangerously decayed tree threatening to fall.

Central to the claim is the requirement that the interference be “unreasonable.” This is an
objective standard, measured not by the plaintiff’s personal sensitivity but by its effect on a
person of ordinary sensibilities. Courts employ a balancing test, weighing the gravity of the
harm inflicted upon the plaintiff against the social utility of the defendant’s conduct. In this
calculus, key factors include the extent, duration, and character of the interference, the
suitability of the activity to its locality, and whether the defendant employed all reasonable
precautions. Consequently, operating a factory in an industrial district may be deemed
reasonable, whereas generating identical noise and smoke in a residential neighborhood likely
is not.

The harm suffered must also be “substantial,” meaning it materially and significantly affects
the property’s comfort, health, or usability, beyond a mere trifling annoyance. Furthermore,
standing is strictly limited to individuals possessing a property interest in the affected land,
such as owners or tenants; a mere guest or visitor lacks the legal right to sue. Successful
plaintiffs may seek two primary remedies. Compensatory damages are awarded for past and
ongoing harms, including property value reduction, lost rental income, and personal
discomfort. Alternatively, or in addition, a court may issue an injunction—a discretionary order
commanding the defendant to abate the nuisance. Courts hesitate to grant injunctions where
the hardship to the defendant and community would be grossly disproportionate to the
plaintiff’s benefit, sometimes awarding “damages in lieu of an injunction.” In narrowly defined
situations, a plaintiff may engage in reasonable self-help, such as cutting intruding branches,
though this approach carries legal risk if exercised improperly.

content.passageText:
XIV. The constitutional architecture of Indian federalism ingeniously embeds a mechanism for
the periodic recalibration of fiscal power between the Union and the States: the Finance
Commission. Established under Article 280, this quasi-judicial body serves as the linchpin of
vertical and horizontal devolution, tasked with ensuring a structured and principled distribution
of national resources. Its primary mandate is to recommend the division of the net proceeds of
taxes between the Centre and the States and the allocation of the States’ share among
themselves. This process, repeated every five years, is not merely an accounting exercise but a
profound exercise in balancing the principles of equity, efficiency, and need within a vast and
diverse federation.

The Commission’s work is fundamentally guided by the constitutional directive to foster
"equitable sharing" based on an objective assessment of states' fiscal capacities and needs. This
involves complex considerations, weighing factors like income distance, geographical area,
and population to address horizontal imbalances. A state with lower per capita income, for
instance, may receive a higher share to equalize its capacity to provide public services.
Simultaneously, the Commission must ensure the Union government retains sufficient fiscal
space to discharge its responsibilities for national defense, foreign affairs, and macroeconomic
stability—a constant tension at the heart of its deliberations. The recommendations extend


beyond tax devolution to encompass grants-in-aid, providing crucial support to states with
revenue deficits or specific needs that the formula cannot fully address.

The evolution of the Finance Commission’s role mirrors India’s changing economic and
political landscape. Initially focused on bridging budgetary gaps, its terms of reference have
expanded to incorporate contemporary challenges like promoting fiscal discipline, funding
local governance institutions, and addressing new priorities like disaster management. Each
Commission thus interprets its constitutional mandate through a contemporary lens, navigating
the competing demands of assertive states and a Union government with pan-national
responsibilities. Its success lies in its non-political, expert-driven approach, which lends
legitimacy to its often-contested recommendations. Ultimately, the Finance Commission is
more than a fiscal arbitrator; it is a vital institution of cooperative federalism, striving to
translate constitutional principles of unity and shared prosperity into a working financial
formula that holds a vast and unequal union together.

             purpose schemes like the PMGSY.

             of sound finance.

content.passageText:
XIV. The constitutional architecture of Indian federalism ingeniously embeds a mechanism for
the periodic recalibration of fiscal power between the Union and the States: the Finance
Commission. Established under Article 280, this quasi-judicial body serves as the linchpin of
vertical and horizontal devolution, tasked with ensuring a structured and principled distribution
of national resources. Its primary mandate is to recommend the division of the net proceeds of
taxes between the Centre and the States and the allocation of the States’ share among
themselves. This process, repeated every five years, is not merely an accounting exercise but a
profound exercise in balancing the principles of equity, efficiency, and need within a vast and
diverse federation.

The Commission’s work is fundamentally guided by the constitutional directive to foster
"equitable sharing" based on an objective assessment of states' fiscal capacities and needs. This
involves complex considerations, weighing factors like income distance, geographical area,
and population to address horizontal imbalances. A state with lower per capita income, for
instance, may receive a higher share to equalize its capacity to provide public services.
Simultaneously, the Commission must ensure the Union government retains sufficient fiscal
space to discharge its responsibilities for national defense, foreign affairs, and macroeconomic
stability—a constant tension at the heart of its deliberations. The recommendations extend


beyond tax devolution to encompass grants-in-aid, providing crucial support to states with
revenue deficits or specific needs that the formula cannot fully address.

The evolution of the Finance Commission’s role mirrors India’s changing economic and
political landscape. Initially focused on bridging budgetary gaps, its terms of reference have
expanded to incorporate contemporary challenges like promoting fiscal discipline, funding
local governance institutions, and addressing new priorities like disaster management. Each
Commission thus interprets its constitutional mandate through a contemporary lens, navigating
the competing demands of assertive states and a Union government with pan-national
responsibilities. Its success lies in its non-political, expert-driven approach, which lends
legitimacy to its often-contested recommendations. Ultimately, the Finance Commission is
more than a fiscal arbitrator; it is a vital institution of cooperative federalism, striving to
translate constitutional principles of unity and shared prosperity into a working financial
formula that holds a vast and unequal union together.

XVIII. At a United Nations meeting about climate change, 16-year-old Greta Thunberg gave a
passionate and angry speech. She criticized people who haven't done enough to stop global
warming. Some people didn't like her speech because they thought her anger would push away
people who might otherwise support the cause. While anger can sometimes make people feel
left out or uncomfortable, many feel Thunberg's anger makes sense. After all, years of pollution
and industrial growth got us into this crisis.
Thunberg's speech highlights a long-standing debate. On one side are people who think anger
is harmful because it doesn't help solve problems. On the other side are those who believe anger
is a natural and useful emotion, both in public life and personal situations. We see this question
come up again and again—from the righteous, worldwide anger that launched the 2017
Women’s March, the day after Donald Trump’s inauguration as president of the United States,
to the violent protests in Hong Kong, to the fearful demonstrations against a new citizenship
law in India. The basic question is always: Is anger useful?
The ancient philosopher Aristotle described anger as a painful feeling that makes us want
revenge when we or someone close to us is treated unfairly. Anger is a reaction to something
that feels wrong, and it includes a desire for payback. Think about when someone you trusted
lied to you, or when your favorite bike was stolen. It hurt, but it also made you feel like you
deserved an explanation.


Modern philosopher Amia Srinivasan argues that anger has real value. She explains that anger
can help people understand their own suffering better. When victims of injustice feel angry,
their emotions become sharper and help them focus on exactly what was done to them. This
anger can actually help them make sense of their situation and understand their oppression
more clearly.
[Extracted with revisions and edits from “The fruits of anger”, aeon.]

XVIII. At a United Nations meeting about climate change, 16-year-old Greta Thunberg gave a
passionate and angry speech. She criticized people who haven't done enough to stop global
warming. Some people didn't like her speech because they thought her anger would push away
people who might otherwise support the cause. While anger can sometimes make people feel
left out or uncomfortable, many feel Thunberg's anger makes sense. After all, years of pollution
and industrial growth got us into this crisis.
Thunberg's speech highlights a long-standing debate. On one side are people who think anger
is harmful because it doesn't help solve problems. On the other side are those who believe anger
is a natural and useful emotion, both in public life and personal situations. We see this question
come up again and again—from the righteous, worldwide anger that launched the 2017
Women’s March, the day after Donald Trump’s inauguration as president of the United States,
to the violent protests in Hong Kong, to the fearful demonstrations against a new citizenship
law in India. The basic question is always: Is anger useful?
The ancient philosopher Aristotle described anger as a painful feeling that makes us want
revenge when we or someone close to us is treated unfairly. Anger is a reaction to something
that feels wrong, and it includes a desire for payback. Think about when someone you trusted
lied to you, or when your favorite bike was stolen. It hurt, but it also made you feel like you
deserved an explanation.

more clearly.

XIX. India spends only 0.6% of its GDP on research and development—far less than China's
2.4% and Brazil's 1.3%. Even more troubling, private companies contribute just one-third of
this amount. If India wants to become a global economic leader, this must change dramatically.


The government has shown commitment through initiatives like the ₹1 lakh crore Research,
Development and Innovation Scheme announced in the 2025-26 Budget. This includes funding
for deep-tech investments, support for the National Quantum Mission, and continued backing
for semiconductor manufacturing. These steps aim to strengthen India's research ecosystem.
Yet private companies remain reluctant to invest their own money in R&D. This hesitation
makes sense. The domestic market rarely rewards innovative products with higher prices, and
government procurement doesn't reliably purchase homegrown innovations. A recent RBI
study confirms that corporate investment optimism actually fell in 2024-25.
Look at how innovation happens globally. Private risk capital, combined with public support,
drives major breakthroughs—with companies leading large-scale applied research.
Consider Meta, which operates roughly 600,000 GPUs costing billions. Google plans to double
its computing capacity every six months to meet AI demand. Their deal with Anthropic,
reportedly worth tens of billions, aims to add over a million GPUs by 2026. No government
could match such investment without exhausting its entire R&D budget.
We saw a similar pattern with data centres. Despite government subsidies, significant private
investment only followed after enterprise demand proved the market existed.
For India to transform its R&D landscape, the private sector needs more than government
schemes. It needs confidence that bold risks will be rewarded. Companies must believe that
investing in differentiated technology makes business sense—that innovative products will
find buyers and early adopters.
Creating this enabling environment means aligning market incentives with innovation. When
private firms see that R&D investment directly connects to growth and profits, they will move
from the margins to the mainstream. Only then can India match its industrial ambitions with
world-class research and development.
[Extracted with revisions and edits from “India’s tech ambitions need private sector investment
in R&D. Budget 2026 holds the key”, ThePrint.]

content.passageText:
I. What will you remember Asrani for? Sholay? Abhimaan? Since the death of the veteran actor
was announced, a lot of obituaries and fan-posts on social media have mentioned his iconic
dialogue from Sholay “Hum angrezon ke zamane ke jailer hain” (I am a jailor of the British
era). Asrani acted in more than 300 films in Hindi and Gujarati. Some small, some big.Despite
such a mammoth filmography, if we choose to remember an actor for a specific role/dialogue
from one film, it says something about our viewing of an actor’s body of work. It means that
we have normalised stereotyping him to such an extent that it doesn’t even seem discordant
anymore. Imagine the disappointment of the actor who is remembered for one role despite a
vast filmography, while marginalising everything else he has done on screen!

On TV shows and public events, Asrani was constantly asked to mouth the Sholay dialogue,
sometimes to his irritation, which he didn’t hide. This dialogue is also entrenched in public
memory because repetition doesn’t allow forgetting. Actors play along to not appear rude and
to entertain their fans and stay in the public memory. This also seems the perfect illustration of
the stereotyping of an actor by the industry, which, in turn, gets entrenched in public
imagination, so much so that you refuse to think of the actor beyond that particular point of
reference. Asrani is one of the many who unwillingly submitted to this stereotype of the funny,
comic actor. He could carry those roles with elan, but what other choice did Asrani have? To
survive in the industry, you perform what is given to you. Audiences are the losers when an
actor is boxed into a slot and denied the opportunity to essay a wide array of roles. Asrani
became a perennial comic.
The Asrani story also makes us think about the fate of an actor in Hindi cinema. That so little
of your filmography is under your control, especially when you don’t look a certain way. The
Bollywood hero has to subscribe to a pre-determined template. When you don’t conform to the
template, you become a character actor — another coinage that makes no sense. Every actor,
including the lead of the film, is playing a character. So why divide and relegate? Here again,
Asrani did not have a choice.

stereotype-101761318585907.html#google_vignette

such a mammoth filmography, if we choose to remember an actor for a specific role/dialogue
from one film, it says something about our viewing of an actor’s body of work. It means that
we have normalised stereotyping him to such an extent that it doesn’t even seem discordant
anymore. Imagine the disappointment of the actor who is remembered for one role despite a
vast filmography, while marginalising everything else he has done on screen!

On TV shows and public events, Asrani was constantly asked to mouth the Sholay dialogue,
sometimes to his irritation, which he didn’t hide. This dialogue is also entrenched in public
memory because repetition doesn’t allow forgetting. Actors play along to not appear rude and
to entertain their fans and stay in the public memory. This also seems the perfect illustration of
the stereotyping of an actor by the industry, which, in turn, gets entrenched in public
imagination, so much so that you refuse to think of the actor beyond that particular point of
reference. Asrani is one of the many who unwillingly submitted to this stereotype of the funny,
comic actor. He could carry those roles with elan, but what other choice did Asrani have? To
survive in the industry, you perform what is given to you. Audiences are the losers when an
actor is boxed into a slot and denied the opportunity to essay a wide array of roles. Asrani
became a perennial comic.

of your filmography is under your control, especially when you don’t look a certain way. The
Bollywood hero has to subscribe to a pre-determined template. When you don’t conform to the
template, you become a character actor — another coinage that makes no sense. Every actor,
including the lead of the film, is playing a character. So why divide and relegate? Here again,
Asrani did not have a choice.

II. Everyone warned me about my new neighbourhood before I moved in. “Not safe.” “Too
immigrant.” “A no-go area.” The labels came thick and casual, like weather talk. I had just
landed in Germany with two squeaky suitcases and a folder full of proofs of existence —
contracts, passport photos, bank statements — ready to start a fellowship in Berlin. I signed the
lease anyway.
My flat is in Neukölln, a district in south Berlin where many Arab and Turkish families have
built their lives over decades. Think of it as the Malviya Nagar of Delhi or Park Circus of
Kolkata — dense, diverse, argumentative, generous. If you’ve never been to Germany, picture
kebab shops and bakeries lining long, straight roads; a wide canal cutting through like a green
ribbon; the metro train — breathing people up and down stairways; and languages braided in
the air —German, Arabic, Turkish, English, and the shy Bengali I carry inside me.
On my first evening, the street met me like a crowded family photo. A football rolled into a
florist’s bucket; roses rocked; the boy apologised; the shopkeeper laughed. A bakery slid open
its shutter; the air filled with sesame and cardamom. The phrase “no-go” didn’t fit anywhere in
my head. In those early days, I learned more German from shopkeepers than from any app. At
the corner store, a cheerful “Kartenzahlung?”— card payment? — taught me how to pay
without holding up the line. At the grocer’s, the aunty weighed parsley and slipped mint into
my bag “for tea, Geschenk”— a gift. At the barber, “Habibi, next week—fresh cut!”.
Berlin’s bureaucracy is famous, and it arrived in my mailbox with insurance letters,
registrations, deadlines. When one envelope stumped me, I carried it to the corner shop like a
broken toy. The owner read it carefully, made two phone calls, and dictated my reply. When I
offered a chocolate bar in thanks, he waved it away. “Neighbour,” he said. That one word did
what no glossy “Welcome to Berlin” brochure could. The longer I live here, the more I think
the only true “no-go” zone is the temptation to speak about a neighbourhood without letting it
speak back. I learned neighbourliness by doing it, until it settled in my muscles: holding
parcels, translating letters, swapping recipes, noticing when a routine goes quiet. Home, and
even the address I claim, isn’t a certificate; it’s the people who answer when I knock.
SOURCE:https://indianexpress.com/article/opinion/columns/germany-immigrants-berlin-
who-is-my-neighbour-neighbourhood-10320831/

III. The most revealing moments in politics are rarely the ones that end careers. They are the
ones that do not. When a leader survives a week of open dissent, hostile headlines, and whispers
of rebellion, it is tempting to call it a victory. But such episodes usually mark something more
ambiguous: a pause in the argument about authority, not its resolution. British Prime Minister
Keir Starmer’s latest brush with political danger fits that pattern. He has emerged still in office,
publicly backed by his cabinet and potential rivals, and determined to project resolve. Yet the
drama that unfolded around him was not a freak storm. It was the product of accumulated
doubts ~ about judgement, about instinct, and about the way power is exercised at the centre.
At the heart of the crisis lay a question that modern governments keep failing to answer
convincingly: how much risk is acceptable in the name of experience, loyalty, or convenience?
The controversy over a senior appointment was not just about one individual’s past
associations. It was about whether the government’s sense of caution had been dulled by the
pressure to move fast and look decisive. When assurances replace hard scrutiny, leaders do not
merely gamble with reputations; they gamble with their own credibility. The response made
things worse before it made them better. Attempts to control the pace and scope of disclosure
signalled defensiveness at precisely the moment when candour was needed. When members of
the governing party begin to force the issue from inside, it is usually because they believe the
leadership has misread both the facts and the mood. That is not rebellion for sport; it is a
warning flare.
For now, the Prime Minister survives because his colleagues have concluded that a leadership
contest would be more damaging than uneasy unity. That is a negative mandate: support rooted
in fear of the alternative rather than confidence in the present. Such arrangements are fragile.
They depend on the absence of new shocks, not the presence of renewed trust. In the end, the
real question is not whether the Prime Minister can cling on. It is whether he can replace a
politics of narrow escapes with one of steadier confidence.
SOURCE: https://www.thestatesman.com/opinion/narrow-survival-1503556602.html

content.passageText:
IV. Little Mrs. Sommers one day found herself the unexpected possessor of fifteen dollars. It
seemed to her a very large amount of money, and the way in which it stuffed and bulged her
worn old porte-monnaie gave her a feeling of importance such as she had not enjoyed for years.
The question of investment was one that occupied her greatly. For a day or two she walked
about apparently in a dreamy state, but really absorbed in speculation and calculation. She did
not wish to act hastily, to do anything she might afterward regret. But it was during the still
hours of the night when she lay awake revolving plans in her mind that she seemed to see her
way clearly toward a proper and judicious use of the money.
A dollar or two should be added to the price usually paid for Janie's shoes, which would insure
their lasting an appreciable time longer than they usually did. She would buy so and so many
yards of percale for new shirt waists for the boys and Janie and Mag. She had intended to make
the old ones do by skilful patching. Mag should have another gown. She had seen some
beautiful patterns, veritable bargains in the shop windows. And still there would be left enough
for new stockings--two pairs apiece--and what darning that would save for a while! She would
get caps for the boys and sailor-hats for the girls. The vision of her little brood looking fresh
and dainty and new for once in their lives excited her and made her restless and wakeful with
anticipation.
The neighbors sometimes talked of certain "better days" that little Mrs. Sommers had known
before she had ever thought of being Mrs. Sommers. She herself indulged in no such morbid
retrospection. She had no time--no second of time to devote to the past. The needs of the present
absorbed her every faculty. A vision of the future like some dim, gaunt monster sometimes
appalled her, but luckily tomorrow never comes.
SOURCE:           https://americanliterature.com/author/kate-chopin/short-story/a-pair-of-silk-
stockings

V. Economics has a fairly straightforward approach to identifying bubbles. Principally, three
criteria must be met for a financial market boom to be classified as a bubble. One, investors
must chase a new asset class where there is no precedent for valuation. Two, there must be
consensus that the object of investor pursuit is the next big thing. Three, returns on investment
become unanchored from earnings. The market frenzy over AI satisfies all three criteria.
Unsurprisingly, murmurs of a bust are getting louder. But this is where economics fails to
provide any further guidance. It has no deterministic criterion to predict when a bubble will
pop. The science, though, becomes more sanguine after a financial crash. It's been the same
story since the tulip mania, possibly even earlier.
AI differs from all productivity-enhancing technologies that have preceded it in its economic
impact. If it delivers, it will replace not just a section but an overwhelming majority of workers.
Success here has severe economic consequences. Incomes would diverge uncontrollably
between the AI-enabled and AI-deprived. Signals from the broader market are flashing orange
as politics drives sound economics off the cliff. AI has concentrated the world's investment
appetite on an unprecedented scale. Its failure, of course, would bring about the biggest wealth
destruction in history.
There is enough economic literature on stages of a bubble, and investors will have to navigate
the current one with a set of incomplete tools. The promise of AI itself is indeterminate, with
lawmakers yet to decide how much of a free run the technology will be allowed. If they manage
to tame the beast - by averting widespread job losses - the returns on current investment will
be watered down. On its part, if AI has, indeed, been oversold, it could create the infrastructure
for productivity enhancement through less disruptive technologies down the line. Investors
must heed the Cassandras. But doom may not be nigh.

provide any further guidance. It has no deterministic criterion to predict when a bubble will
pop. The science, though, becomes more sanguine after a financial crash. It's been the same
story since the tulip mania, possibly even earlier.
AI differs from all productivity-enhancing technologies that have preceded it in its economic
impact. If it delivers, it will replace not just a section but an overwhelming majority of workers.
Success here has severe economic consequences. Incomes would diverge uncontrollably
between the AI-enabled and AI-deprived. Signals from the broader market are flashing orange
as politics drives sound economics off the cliff. AI has concentrated the world's investment
appetite on an unprecedented scale. Its failure, of course, would bring about the biggest wealth
destruction in history.
There is enough economic literature on stages of a bubble, and investors will have to navigate
the current one with a set of incomplete tools. The promise of AI itself is indeterminate, with
lawmakers yet to decide how much of a free run the technology will be allowed. If they manage
to tame the beast - by averting widespread job losses - the returns on current investment will
be watered down. On its part, if AI has, indeed, been oversold, it could create the infrastructure
for productivity enhancement through less disruptive technologies down the line. Investors
must heed the Cassandras. But doom may not be nigh.

in-an-ai-bubble/articleshow/124790383.cms?from=mdr

maintain international peace and security through collective action among states. However, critics
increasingly argue that the organisation has struggled to effectively prevent or end modern conflicts.
Wars in regions such as Ukraine, Gaza, and parts of Africa have revived debates about the UN’s
structural limitations. A major criticism concerns the veto power held by the five permanent members
of the UN Security Council — the United States, Russia, China, the United Kingdom, and France —
which often leads to deadlock when major powers are involved in conflicts. Many developing countries
argue that the global governance system reflects post-1945 power structures and disproportionately
represents Western interests. As a result, calls for UN Security Council reform have intensified, with
countries like India, Brazil, Germany, and Japan advocating expanded permanent membership. Despite
its limitations, the UN continues to play an important role in peacekeeping operations, humanitarian
assistance, and international diplomacy.

content.passageText:
Legal Reasoning


XI. The genesis of India's Constitution lies in the historic deliberations of its Constituent
Assembly. A critical legal and historical fact is that this Assembly was not a spontaneous
creation but was established under a specific constitutional framework. Contrary to common
misconception, it was not formed by the Indian Independence Act of 1947, though that act later
granted it sovereign power. The Assembly's foundational basis was also not the prevailing
Government of India Act of 1935, which it was meant to replace, nor was it the Objectives
Resolution, which was one of its own early products. Rather, the Constituent Assembly was
concretely set up under the provisions of the Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946. This Plan,
formulated by three British ministers, proposed the composition and method of election for the
Assembly, envisioning it as the body to draft a constitution for a united India. Thus, its very
existence and initial structure were derived from this 1946 plan.


Following this framework, the first meeting of the Constituent Assembly was convened on
December 9, 1946. The session was marked by the notable absence of members from the
Muslim League, who boycotted the proceedings. Despite this significant political challenge
and the shadow of impending partition, the Assembly's work began. The most immediate and
crucial outcome of this inaugural session was not the adoption of the National Flag or the
Objectives Resolution, both of which occurred in later sessions, nor was it the appointment of
the Drafting Committee, which came much later in August 1947. The paramount achievement
was the election of Dr. Rajendra Prasad as the Permanent President of the Assembly on
December 11, 1946. This election provided the Assembly with stable and respected leadership,
ensuring its procedural continuity and legitimacy at a very fragile moment. By successfully
constituting itself with a permanent presiding officer, the Assembly demonstrated its
operational viability and set the essential administrative foundation for the monumental task
ahead, navigating the complex journey from a British blueprint to an independent Republic.

The Government of India Act, 1935

The Objectives Resolution, 1946

content.passageText:
XII. A breach of contract under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, triggers a suite of remedial
options for the aggrieved party, primarily outlined in Sections 73 to 75. These provisions
establish a comprehensive framework designed not to punish the defaulting party, but to
compensate the injured party for the loss suffered and, where possible, to uphold the sanctity
of the original agreement.


The principal remedy is an award of damages under Section 73. The foundational principle is
to place the plaintiff in the same financial position they would have occupied had the contract
been performed. This covers ordinary damages, which arise naturally in the usual course of
events from the breach. For special damages—losses arising from the plaintiff’s particular
circumstances—the defendant must have had knowledge, actual or imputed, of those
circumstances at the time of contract formation, ensuring the loss was within the parties’
contemplation. Section 74 addresses liquidated damages, a genuine pre-estimate of loss
stipulated in the contract itself. The critical distinction lies in the court’s treatment of a penalty,
which is a stipulation in terrorem to secure performance. While Section 74 permits recovery of
the stipulated sum whether termed penalty or damages, the amount awarded is limited to the
court’s assessment of the actual loss or injury proved, never exceeding the stipulated figure,
thereby neutralizing penal consequences.


Beyond monetary compensation, equitable remedies seek to enforce performance directly.
Specific Performance, governed by the Specific Relief Act, 1963, is a discretionary decree
ordering the defendant to execute their contractual promise, typically granted where damages
are inadequate, as in contracts concerning unique property. Similarly, an Injunction, a
restraining order, prevents a party from committing a breach negative in nature, such as
violating a non-compete covenant.


Finally, the doctrine of Quantum Meruit operates on principles of quasi-contract to prevent
unjust enrichment. Where a contract is discharged by breach or becomes void, and a party has
executed a part, they can claim reasonable remuneration for the work done or benefits
conferred. This ensures fairness, allowing recovery for value delivered even in the absence of
a fully executed agreement. Together, these remedies under Sections 73-75 provide a balanced
and just system for addressing contractual breaches, blending compensatory, deterrent, and
restorative principles.

XIII. The Indian Constitution establishes a bicameral Union Parliament, comprising the
directly elected Lok Sabha (House of the People) and the Rajya Sabha (Council of States),
representing the states. State legislatures are predominantly unicameral, with a few retaining a
Legislative Council as their upper house. These bodies wield the core legislative power of the
Union and States respectively, as demarcated by the Seventh Schedule’s Union, State, and
Concurrent Lists. Beyond lawmaking, they exercise critical financial control through the
sanction of expenditures and taxation, and hold the executive accountable via mechanisms like
questions, debates, and no-confidence motions. To ensure fearless deliberation, legislators
enjoy constitutional privileges under Articles 105 and 194, including freedom of speech within
the house and immunity from prosecution for official proceedings, powers essential for
parliamentary autonomy.


The legislative procedure involves introduction, consideration, and passage of bills in each
house, with the President’s or Governor’s assent required for enactment. A critical exception is
the Money Bill, stringently defined under Article 110. Certified exclusively by the Lok Sabha
Speaker, such bills deal solely with specified financial matters like taxation or Consolidated
Fund expenditure. Their introduction is restricted to the Lok Sabha, and the Rajya Sabha can
only recommend amendments; the lower house holds the final authority, reinforcing the
primacy of the directly elected house in financial legislation. To curb political instability, the
Tenth Schedule (Anti-defection Law) disqualifies members on grounds of voluntarily giving
up party membership or defying a whip on a vote, aiming to preserve the electoral mandate’s
sanctity, though its application has raised complex questions regarding legislative
independence.


The dynamic between parliamentary sovereignty and constitutional supremacy is central to
India’s framework. Unlike the UK, India’s Parliament is not supreme. It operates within limits
set by a written, rigid Constitution, which is the supreme lex. This is vividly demonstrated by
Article 13, which voids laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights, and the Basic Structure
Doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973), which holds that Parliament’s amending power under


Article 368 cannot alter the Constitution’s foundational identity. Thus, while Parliament
possesses expansive legislative and constituent powers, its authority is subordinated to and
constrained by the Constitution, with the judiciary acting as the ultimate interpreter and
guardian of this supreme document, ensuring a delicate balance of power among the sovereign
organs of the state.

content.passageText:
XIV. In a landmark judgment reshaping India's reservation jurisprudence, the Supreme Court
has unequivocally permitted states to enact laws creating sub-classifications within the lists of
Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes for the purpose of distributing reservation benefits.
This ruling fundamentally recalibrates the balance of power between the legislature and the
judiciary on a deeply sensitive social justice issue. At the heart of this legal shift is the Court's
decisive overturning of its own 2004 precedent in E.V. Chinnaiah vs. State of Andhra Pradesh.


The Chinnaiah judgment, delivered by a five-judge Constitution Bench, had imposed a
significant restriction on state authority. It held that the Scheduled Castes, as notified under
Articles 341 and 342 of the Constitution, constituted a single, homogeneous class for the
purpose of Article 16(4). The Court reasoned that any sub-division by a state legislature would
violate the constitutional scheme and the right to equality under Article 14. This precedent had
effectively frozen state-level attempts to ensure that the most backward among the SCs/STs
received a fair share of reservation benefits, as it mandated that all communities within the list
must be treated identically.


The recent verdict, delivered by a seven-judge bench, dismantles this legal barrier. It
authoritatively holds that the Chinnaiah judgment was incorrectly decided. The Court has now
ruled that there is no constitutional prohibition against sub-classification. It affirmed that
inequalities within the SC/ST communities themselves are a stark social reality. When some
groups within these lists have historically cornered a disproportionate share of the reservation
benefits, leaving others in continued backwardness, the state has both a right and a positive
obligation to rectify this internal imbalance. This power, the Court clarified, flows from the
legislature's competence to determine the adequacy of representation under Article 16(4) and
to promote substantive equality. By overturning Chinnaiah, the Supreme Court has restored to
state governments a vital tool for fine-tuning reservation policies to achieve equitable
distribution, moving beyond a one-size-fits-all approach to a more nuanced, needs-based model
for social justice.

XV. The legal landscape for transgender rights in India has been fundamentally shaped by the
Supreme Court's landmark 2014 ruling in National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) v.
Union of India. This judgment expansively interpreted Article 21 of the Constitution, holding
that the right to life and personal liberty inherently includes the right to one's gender identity,
autonomy, and dignity. By recognizing transgender persons as a third gender, the Court
mandated their legal recognition and directed the Centre and State Governments to treat them
as socially and educationally backward classes (OBCs). This pivotal direction made them
eligible for reservation in education and public employment under the existing OBC quota,
rather than creating a separate, fixed-percentage category. This classification was aimed at
providing substantive equality and affirmative action to a historically marginalized community.


However, the subsequent Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019, introduced
provisions that many activists and experts argue regress from the NALSA principles. A widely
criticized feature is the process for obtaining a certificate of identity. Contrary to the self-
determination model affirmed by the Supreme Court, the Act requires an application to the
District Magistrate, who issues a certificate based on a recommendation from a district
screening committee. This medicalized and bureaucratic process is seen as infringing upon the
dignity and autonomy guaranteed by NALSA.


Judicial interpretation has continued to advance transgender rights in specific domains. In Arun
Kumar v. Inspector General of Registration (2022), the Madras High Court addressed the
crucial right to marry. It held that a marriage between a cisgender man and a transgender
woman who had not undergone gender-confirmation surgery constitutes a valid heterosexual
marriage under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. This reasoning, building on a similar 2019 ruling

XV. The legal landscape for transgender rights in India has been fundamentally shaped by the
Supreme Court's landmark 2014 ruling in National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) v.
Union of India. This judgment expansively interpreted Article 21 of the Constitution, holding
that the right to life and personal liberty inherently includes the right to one's gender identity,
autonomy, and dignity. By recognizing transgender persons as a third gender, the Court
mandated their legal recognition and directed the Centre and State Governments to treat them
as socially and educationally backward classes (OBCs). This pivotal direction made them
eligible for reservation in education and public employment under the existing OBC quota,
rather than creating a separate, fixed-percentage category. This classification was aimed at
providing substantive equality and affirmative action to a historically marginalized community.


However, the subsequent Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019, introduced
provisions that many activists and experts argue regress from the NALSA principles. A widely
criticized feature is the process for obtaining a certificate of identity. Contrary to the self-
determination model affirmed by the Supreme Court, the Act requires an application to the
District Magistrate, who issues a certificate based on a recommendation from a district
screening committee. This medicalized and bureaucratic process is seen as infringing upon the
dignity and autonomy guaranteed by NALSA.

Kumar v. Inspector General of Registration (2022), the Madras High Court addressed the
crucial right to marry. It held that a marriage between a cisgender man and a transgender
woman who had not undergone gender-confirmation surgery constitutes a valid heterosexual
marriage under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. This reasoning, building on a similar 2019 ruling
from the same court, validated such unions without requiring explicit legislative amendment,

progressive constitutional interpretation and legislative measures that are perceived as falling
short of guaranteeing full self-determination.

XVI. The statutory framework governing Christian succession in India, primarily enshrined in
the Indian Succession Act, 1925, extends beyond the standard rules of intestate and
testamentary distribution to address specific, often complex, situational doctrines. These
provisions resolve ambiguities and address the status of individuals who occupy a peripheral
position under the default inheritance scheme.


A critical aspect is the succession to a minor’s property. As a minor lacks the legal capacity to
manage assets, the estate of a deceased Christian minor does not vest directly in their natural
guardian. Instead, its administration is governed by the secular Guardians and Wards Act, 1890.
The court, prioritizing the welfare of the minor, will appoint a guardian to manage the inherited
property prudently until the minor attains the age of majority, ensuring the estate is preserved
for their ultimate benefit.


The law adopts a distinct approach towards illegitimate children. Under the Act’s intestacy
rules, an illegitimate child possesses no legal right to inherit from the father’s estate. This
restrictive stance is, however, partially mitigated by the child’s right to succeed to the mother’s
property on her intestacy. Importantly, the principle of testamentary freedom allows a father to
expressly bequeath property to an illegitimate child through a valid will, thereby circumventing
the statutory exclusion.


The doctrine of commorientes addresses the rare but legally significant scenario of
simultaneous death. When two individuals, such as a husband and wife, perish in a common
disaster where the sequence of death cannot be ascertained, Section 21 of the Act establishes a
legal presumption for succession purposes: the younger is deemed to have survived the elder.
This presumption, while crucial for determining the line of inheritance, is rebuttable by direct
evidence proving the actual order of death.


A fundamental principle of property law, escheat, applies when a Christian dies intestate
without leaving any heir identifiable under the succession hierarchy of the Act. In such an
event, where no natural or legal person is entitled to claim the estate, the property does not
remain in abeyance but instead devolves upon the state, thereby preventing title from becoming
dormant.


Finally, the applicability of these rules is profoundly influenced by the concept of domicile.
Succession to movable property for an Indian Christian is governed by the law of their domicile
at the time of death. Consequently, a Christian of Indian origin domiciled abroad may have the
succession to their movable assets determined by foreign law, while their immovable property
in India remains subject to the Indian Succession Act, creating a potential conflict of laws
scenario that requires careful legal navigation within this codified personal law system.

options:

          was his permanent domicile at the time of his death.

          succession to the Mumbai factory will be decided by French civil law.

The succession to both the Paris bank account and the Mumbai factory will be
          governed by the Indian Succession Act, 1925.

The succession to the Mumbai factory will be governed by Indian law, but the
          succession to the Paris bank account will be governed by French law.

the world. Now it has dropped to 20th place. That is the lowest score Britain has ever received
for honesty in government.

happened under Boris Johnson. And all of this was before the latest problems involving Peter
Mandelson. Unless things change quickly, next year’s report will likely be even worse.

and again to “clean up politics.” But his government got off to a bad start. Some of his team
accepted free clothes and tickets to events. They declared these gifts properly, but it still looked
bad. One study found that top Labour officials accepted over £220,000 worth of free tickets
during the last few years. These included tickets to Glastonbury, Wimbledon, and the British
Grand Prix.

handed out billions in contracts. Watchdogs found serious problems in about a third of that
spending. They said it looked like more than just bad luck or mistakes.

government for a bank that later went bust. And George Osborne, another former minister, has
taken many well-paid jobs since leaving office. None of this is illegal. But it makes people
wonder if politicians are working for the public or for themselves.

worse. At a time when politics already feels broken, every little bit of bad news adds up.

XIX. In the town of Millfield, there are five main shops: a bakery, a bookstore, a café, a diner,
   and an emporium. Each shop is owned by one of five individuals: Alice, Bob, Carol, David,
   and Emily. The following facts are known about the shops and owners:
 I.The bakery and the bookstore are both located on Main Street.
II.No shop on Main Street sells clothing.
III.The café and the diner are the only shops that sell food, and they both sell food.
IV.The emporium sells clothing, and it is not on Main Street.


  V.Every owner who owns a shop on Main Street is a member of the Millfield Business
    Association (MBA).
 VI.No member of the MBA owns a shop that sells clothing.
VII.Alice owns the bakery.
VIII.Bob owns a shop that sells food.
 IX.Carol does not own a shop on Main Street.
  X.David owns the emporium.
 XI.Emily owns the bookstore, and she is a member of the MBA.


    Additionally, each shop has a unique three-letter code for its inventory system. The codes for
    some shops are as follows:
        1. Bakery: ABM
        2. Bookstore: EKM
        3. Emporium: DEO


    The codes are formed by taking the first letter of the shop type (B for bakery, K for bookstore,
    C for café, D for diner, E for emporium), the first letter of the owner’s name (A for Alice, B for
    Bob, C for Carol, D for David, E for Emily), and the first letter of the street location (M for
    Main Street, O for other streets), and then arranging these three letters in a specific order. This
    order is consistent for all shops and can be deduced from the given codes.


    Finally, the town is hosting a contest, and each shop has submitted an entry. The rules for the
    contest are:
   i.Any shop that sells food is eligible for the culinary prize.
  ii.Any shop owned by a member of the MBA is eligible for the community prize.
  iii.No shop that sells clothing is eligible for the family prize.
  iv.All shops on Main Street are eligible for the heritage prize.

content.passageText:
XXI. Your fingers might tell a surprising story about the human brain. New research suggests
that the length of your fingers, specifically how they compare to each other, could be linked to
how our brains evolved.


Scientists have long known that human brains have grown larger over time. A new study points
to a possible reason: a hormone called estrogen that babies are exposed to before they are born.


The study focuses on something called the "digit ratio." This is simply a comparison of your
index finger (the one you use to point) and your ring finger. Scientists call this the 2D:4D ratio.


Here is what they have learned. When a baby is growing in the womb, it is exposed to hormones
like estrogen and testosterone. If the baby gets more estrogen relative to testosterone during
the first three months, the index finger tends to be longer than the ring finger. This is called a
high 2D:4D ratio. If there is more testosterone, the ring finger is usually longer, which is a low
ratio.


For this new study, researchers wanted to see if this finger ratio was connected to brain size.
Since the size of a newborn's head is a good way to estimate brain size, they measured the
heads and fingers of 225 babies. The group had 100 boys and 125 girls.


The results showed a clear pattern, but only in the boys. Baby boys with a higher 2D:4D ratio
(meaning more estrogen before birth) also had larger heads. This link was not found in girls.


So, what does this mean for human evolution? Professor John Manning from Swansea
University explains that the drive to have a bigger brain may have come with a trade-off. High
estrogen levels in males (shown by their finger ratio) are also linked to some health issues, like
heart problems, low sperm counts, and a higher risk of schizophrenia.


But a larger brain may have been so important for survival that it made up for these problems.
In other words, the evolution of the human brain may have been helped by the very same
hormone that causes some health risks in men.


This study adds to the idea that the hormone estrogen, received before birth, played a key role
in shaping the human brain, even if it came with some biological costs.


[Extracted with revisions and edits from “Scientists find a clue to human brain evolution in
finger length”, ScienceDaily.]

       skeletal signs.

       ancestors did.

       and skull size.
