content.passageText:
I. The Trump administration has imposed fresh sanctions on Russia as punitive measures
relating to Moscow’s refusal to strike a ceasefire agreement to bring the war in Ukraine to a
halt, with Washington targeting Russian oil giants Rosneft and Lukoil. Russia’s use of the oil
trade to finance war has been a bone of contention for NATO members since the early days of
Russia’s incursion into and attacks on Ukraine, an indirect dimension of the conflict that has
pulled Asian powers India and China into the fray. Over the summer, Mr. Trump sought to up
the ante in this regard by slapping India with an additional 25% tariff for importing Russian
oil, over and above the basic 25% rate imposed on other countries as well, even though China,
as a top importer of Russian seaborne crude, was spared this levy. Now, the latest round of
sanctions appeared to have penalised both trading partners of Moscow significantly, with
reports suggesting that at least four major state-owned Chinese oil companies have suspended
purchases from Russia and that at least one private and three state-owned Indian refinery
companies are planning for “recalibration of Russian oil imports” including the possibility of
a “massive cut” over time.
At the heart of the White House move is the seething frustration of Mr. Trump over failed
attempts to not only bring Russian President Vladimir Putin to the negotiating table — a feat
achieved in Alaska in August and a second summit agreed in Budapest before it was postponed
following the collapse of ceasefire talks — but also to nudge the Kremlin towards at least a
short-term arrangement that might lead to a cessation of hostilities as a precursor to a broader
treaty on territorial and institutional agreements. It is possible that the latest sanctions may lead
to a genuine tightening of options for Mr. Putin on ending the war, especially as Washington
will now be joining the European Union that has adopted its 19th sanctions package against
Moscow, specifically focusing on technology supply chains, energy revenues, and financial
networks. Nevertheless, it may be premature to applaud their potential impact on the Kremlin’s
strategic calculus. Ultimately, whether sanctions have teeth or not depends on the consistency
of their enforcement, including shutting down the inevitable loopholes and workarounds that
Moscow will seek to exploit to continue selling oil abroad, possibly at even sharper discounts.
Mr. Trump may find that he has travelled full circle to arrive at the same sticky negotiating
points between Moscow and Kiev that his predecessor faced — an early end to ground
hostilities, control of Donbas, and the permissible extent of NATO influence in the region. Only
if sanctions can break Russian strategic will on at least one of these points will the prospects
for                        peace                        brighten                         considerably.


SOURCE:https://www.thehindu.com/opinion/editorial/sanctioning-russia-on-the-trump-
administrations-fresh-sanctions-on-russia/article70198083.ece

content.passageText:
I. The Trump administration has imposed fresh sanctions on Russia as punitive measures
relating to Moscow’s refusal to strike a ceasefire agreement to bring the war in Ukraine to a
halt, with Washington targeting Russian oil giants Rosneft and Lukoil. Russia’s use of the oil
trade to finance war has been a bone of contention for NATO members since the early days of
Russia’s incursion into and attacks on Ukraine, an indirect dimension of the conflict that has
pulled Asian powers India and China into the fray. Over the summer, Mr. Trump sought to up
the ante in this regard by slapping India with an additional 25% tariff for importing Russian
oil, over and above the basic 25% rate imposed on other countries as well, even though China,
as a top importer of Russian seaborne crude, was spared this levy. Now, the latest round of
sanctions appeared to have penalised both trading partners of Moscow significantly, with
reports suggesting that at least four major state-owned Chinese oil companies have suspended
purchases from Russia and that at least one private and three state-owned Indian refinery
companies are planning for “recalibration of Russian oil imports” including the possibility of
a “massive cut” over time.
At the heart of the White House move is the seething frustration of Mr. Trump over failed
attempts to not only bring Russian President Vladimir Putin to the negotiating table — a feat
achieved in Alaska in August and a second summit agreed in Budapest before it was postponed
following the collapse of ceasefire talks — but also to nudge the Kremlin towards at least a
short-term arrangement that might lead to a cessation of hostilities as a precursor to a broader
treaty on territorial and institutional agreements. It is possible that the latest sanctions may lead
to a genuine tightening of options for Mr. Putin on ending the war, especially as Washington
will now be joining the European Union that has adopted its 19th sanctions package against
Moscow, specifically focusing on technology supply chains, energy revenues, and financial
networks. Nevertheless, it may be premature to applaud their potential impact on the Kremlin’s
strategic calculus. Ultimately, whether sanctions have teeth or not depends on the consistency
of their enforcement, including shutting down the inevitable loopholes and workarounds that
Moscow will seek to exploit to continue selling oil abroad, possibly at even sharper discounts.
Mr. Trump may find that he has travelled full circle to arrive at the same sticky negotiating
points between Moscow and Kiev that his predecessor faced — an early end to ground
hostilities, control of Donbas, and the permissible extent of NATO influence in the region. Only
if sanctions can break Russian strategic will on at least one of these points will the prospects
for                        peace                        brighten                         considerably.

administrations-fresh-sanctions-on-russia/article70198083.ece

II. Nikolay Tchikildyeev, a waiter in the Moscow hotel, Slavyansky Bazaar, was taken ill. His
legs went numb and his gait was affected, so that on one occasion, as he was going along the
corridor, he tumbled and fell down with a tray full of ham and peas. He had to leave his job.
All his own savings and his wife's were spent on doctors and medicines; they had nothing left
to live upon. He felt dull with no work to do, and he made up his mind he must go home to the
village. It is better to be ill at home, and living there is cheaper; and it is a true saying that the
walls of home are a help.
He reached Zhukovo towards evening. In his memories of childhood he had pictured his home
as bright, snug, comfortable. Now, going into the hut, he was positively frightened; it was so
dark, so crowded, so unclean. His wife Olga and his daughter Sasha, who had come with him,
kept looking in bewilderment at the big untidy stove, which filled up almost half the hut and
was black with soot and flies. What lots of flies! The stove was on one side, the beams lay
slanting on the walls, and it looked as though the hut were just going to fall to pieces. In the
corner, facing the door, under the holy images, bottle labels and newspaper cuttings were stuck
on the walls instead of pictures. The poverty, the poverty!
Of the grown-up people there were none at home; all were at work at the harvest. On the stove
was sitting a white-headed girl of eight, unwashed and apathetic; she did not even glance at
them as they came in. On the floor a white cat was rubbing itself against the oven fork.
"Puss, puss!" Sasha called to her. "Puss!"
"She can't hear," said the little girl; "she has gone deaf."
"How is that?"
"Oh, she was beaten."


Nikolay and Olga realized from the first glance what life was like here, but said nothing to one
another; in silence they put down their bundles, and went out into the village street. Their hut
was the third from the end, and seemed the very poorest and oldest-looking; the second was
not much better; but the last one had an iron roof, and curtains in the windows. That hut stood
apart, not enclosed; it was a tavern. The huts were in a single row, and the whole of the little
village -- quiet and dreamy, with willows, elders, and mountain-ash trees peeping out from the
yards -- had an attractive look.


SOURCE: https://americanliterature.com/author/anton-chekhov/short-story/peasants

III. India, vibrant and diverse, revels in its festivals. But behind the celebrations lies an
unpleasant truth: almost every festival leaves a heavy, relentless trail of pollution. Chhath Puja
starts today, and rivers and water bodies are set to bear the brunt. Even though many idols -
Durga, Ganesh, etc - use eco-friendly colours, add-ons like plastics, aluminium foil and fabric
pollute rivers, harm aquatic life and upset delicate ecosystems. Noise pollution remains the
silent bane of India.
Pollution also feeds convenient politics. BJP sparring with AAP in Delhi over chemicals used
to clear the Yamuna's foamy mess is just one example. Across India, irrespective of party
colour, governments have failed to address environmental decay. It's not even an election issue.
With every passing year and festival, the situation worsens. This Diwali, when tracking
dangerous pollution peaks was critical, majority of Delhi's 39 continuous ambient air quality
monitoring stations went offline for hours, leaving major data gaps. Even the few functioning
stations faced blackouts of 1-9 hrs during the crucial 36-hr window between midnight Monday
and 11 a.m. on Tuesday.
Yet, the responsibility does not rest with governments alone. Citizens, too, must shoulder the
blame for thoughtlessly contributing to environmental degradation - whether polluting rivers,
neglecting urban waste or disregarding the impact on children, the elderly and those with
disabilities like autism, and facilitating the distress of animals. Festivals are meant to celebrate
life, not compromise it. As Chhath Puja unfolds, the citizenry and state should stop making our
festivals seem hardwired to civic pain. Instead, bring back the truth in the old adage: cleanliness
is                           next                             to                          godliness.

next-to-godliness/articleshow/124790425.cms?from=mdr

content.passageText:
V. WHAT DO women really carry around in their just-in-case purse: lipstick, pepper spray, two
snacks, a tampon, three tissues… If Mary Poppins were Indian, she would be every woman
with a tote bag. Unlike the men in their lives, whose pockets hold, maybe, a phone and a wallet,
women’s purses carry universes inside them. The bags aren’t simply accessories; they are
portable archives of responsibility, preparedness and a little bit of magic.
The insides of a purse may seem like clutter, but it isn’t. It’s a labour of love, fear and foresight
translated into objects. Each just-in-case item is a woman’s way of carrying not just herself,
but everyone she cares about. But why do women do this? Because they are conditioned to live
in the land of just-in-case. Just in case someone falls sick, just in case a child cries, just in case
the car breaks down. The purse is less about fashion and more about forethought. An invisible
syllabus of caregiving tucked into zippers.
From a psychological lens, the just-in-case purse isn’t about objects; it reflects the mental load
women carry every day. Research shows that women are often socialised into anticipatory
caregiving; they not only respond to needs, but also predict them. The Band-Aid is for the
scrapes that haven’t happened yet, the snacks for a hunger no one has admitted to yet and the
tissues for tears not yet cried.
Entire industries thrive on the idea that women must always be prepared. Cosmetics, fashion
and lifestyle brands have mastered the art of packaging responsibility into something portable.
The travel perfume that promises confidence, the compact powder that claims to save face, the
foldable flats marketed as a rescue from heels that betray you at midnight. None of these are
sold as luxuries. They are sold as safeguards. Preparedness becomes something that can be
purchased, wrapped in glossy packaging, and tucked neatly into a handbag. This expectation
turns resilience into a market. What looks like empowerment is often pressure in disguise,
urging women to buy not just products, but a sense of peace of mind. The just-in-case purse,
then, is not simply about habit or preference. It is a cultural construct, shaped as much by
advertising as by tradition, tying identity to preparedness and responsibility to consumption

V. In a move that challenges the very spirit of free inquiry, Government of India (GoI) has
asked ministries to revisit how PhD guides are chosen and to steer doctoral research toward
innovation, national priorities and stronger academia—industry collaboration. While closer ties
with industry are desirable, the zealous drive to accelerate R&D— from dictating who can
guide to what may be researched—risks stifling academic freedom.
For a country racing to catch up in the global innovation sweepstakes, the temptation to direct
research toward state-declared priorities is understandable. After all, central planning of
research yielded visible results in China and the erstwhile Soviet Union. But those models came
with a heavy cost—narrowing the field of enquiry, silencing unconventional thought, and often
discouraging the very curiosity that fuels genuine discovery. No matter how well-intentioned,
a ‘helping hand’ that steers too tightly ends up throttling what it seeks to nurture.
A state-approved list of research themes or mentors would push aside ‘non-priority’ areas —
the arts, humanities, and blue-sky sciences that often yield breakthroughs because they wander
off the beaten path. Innovation rarely flourishes under supervision. It thrives in the freely
explored, where failure is tolerated and curiosity unrestrained. Academic freedom is not an
indulgence; it is the oxygen of progress and the foundation on which great nations build their
scientific and cultural capital. India’s challenge is to find that balance between guiding research
and granting freedom. GoI should identify national priorities and channel more incentives
toward them. But that must come as an invitation, not an instruction. The record worldwide is
clear: chokeholds on research do not produce results — freedom, diversity, and a culture that
celebrates                                      questioning                                     do.

VII. In 2026, India witnessed renewed public debate on passive euthanasia following the widely
reported case of Harish Rana, which brought end-of-life rights back into focus. Passive euthanasia refers
to the withdrawal or withholding of life-sustaining treatment in cases where recovery is deemed
unlikely, allowing a patient to die naturally. The Supreme Court of India had previously recognised
passive euthanasia as legally permissible under strict safeguards, particularly through its landmark
judgments that affirmed the right to die with dignity as part of Article 21. The Harish Rana case
highlighted practical challenges in implementing advance directives (living wills), consent procedures,
and hospital protocols. It also raised ethical questions regarding patient autonomy, medical
responsibility, and the role of family members in decision-making. The case reignited discussions on
whether India should move towards clearer statutory regulation of end-of-life care, balancing
constitutional rights with safeguards against misuse.

Source: The Hindu

Legal Reasoning


IX. Sentencing and punishment under the Indian Penal Code, 1860, form the cornerstone of
India’s retributive and reformative criminal justice system. Section 53 of the IPC enumerates
the permissible punishments, creating a hierarchical and discretionary framework for courts to
impose penalties commensurate with the gravity of the offence. The types of punishments
include Death Penalty, Life Imprisonment, Imprisonment (which may be rigorous or simple),
Forfeiture of Property, and Fine. These sanctions are not mutually exclusive; often, fines are
imposed in conjunction with imprisonment.
The most severe sanction, the death penalty, is reserved for the “rarest of rare” cases, a doctrinal
limitation crafted by the Supreme Court in the landmark case of Bachan Singh v. State of
Punjab (1980). This doctrine mandates that capital punishment is an exception, not the rule, to
be invoked only when the alternative of life imprisonment is “unquestionably foreclosed.” The
court must balance aggravating and mitigating circumstances of the crime and the criminal,
ensuring the sentence is proportionate. Its application is typically confined to certain forms of
aggravated murder and terrorism-related offences. The procedure is also meticulously
safeguarded, requiring confirmation by a High Court and affording the convict multiple
avenues of appeal and mercy petitions.
Life imprisonment, often misunderstood as incarceration for a precise term, generally means
imprisonment for the remainder of the convict’s natural life, though remissions and parole
mechanisms exist. Imprisonment is bifurcated into rigorous and simple. Rigorous
imprisonment involves compulsory hard labour, while simple imprisonment entails
confinement without such labour, prescribed for less severe offences. Forfeiture of property, a
consequential penalty, involves the confiscation of assets and is sometimes specified for certain
crimes against the state. Lastly, a fine can be a sole punishment or a supplementary one, with
the court possessing the power to impose imprisonment in default of its payment, subject to
statutory limits.
Thus, the IPC provides a structured yet flexible sentencing palette, ranging from the ultimate
sanction of death to pecuniary penalties, guided by principles of proportionality,
individualization, and, in the context of capital punishment, an exceedingly high threshold of
judicial scrutiny. The system continually negotiates the tensions between societal demand for
retribution and the constitutional values of justice and human dignity.

content.passageText:
X. Within the intricate framework of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, several equitable
doctrines operate to ensure justice, clarity, and the effective administration of property rights.
Among these, the Rule Against Perpetuity, the Doctrine of Election, and the Doctrine of Merger
serve as foundational pillars, while the related Doctrine of Cy-pres governs charitable trusts.


The Rule Against Perpetuity, encapsulated in Section 14, is a central pillar of property law
designed to prevent the tying up of property inalienably for an excessive period. It mandates
that no future interest in property is valid unless it must vest, if at all, within a life or lives in
being at the creation of the interest plus twenty-one years, excluding the period of gestation.
This rule strikes a crucial balance between allowing settlors to control the future devolution of
their assets and ensuring that property remains marketable and free from dead-hand control for
generations, thereby serving the public interest by facilitating its circulation in the economy.


The Doctrine of Election, detailed in Section 35, embodies the equitable maxim that one cannot
approbate and reprobate. It stipulates that if an instrument, such as a will or deed, purports to
transfer a property belonging to another person while also conferring a benefit on that same
person, the beneficiary must choose (elect) either to accept the benefit under the instrument,
thereby surrendering their own property, or to retain their own property, forfeiting the conferred
benefit. This doctrine ensures fairness by preventing a person from taking advantage of an
instrument while simultaneously disregarding its dispositive provisions.
Distinct from election, the Doctrine of Merger addresses the confluence of estates. It operates
automatically when a lesser estate and a greater estate in the same property unite in the same
person, in the same right, with no intermediate interest existing between them. For instance, if
a lessee acquires the freehold (ownership) of the leased property, the leasehold interest merges
into the freehold and extinguishes. The intent of the parties may sometimes prevent merger, but
the doctrine's primary purpose is to simplify the title by eliminating superfluous and coexisting
interests held by a single individual.
While the Doctrine of Cy-pres finds its statutory home in the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, it is
conceptually vital in property law concerning charitable trusts. It empowers the court, when
the specific purpose of a charitable trust becomes impossible or impracticable to fulfil, to direct
the trust property to be applied cy-pres (as near as possible) to the original general charitable
intent of the settlor. This prevents the failure of the trust and ensures that charitable resources
continue to serve the public good, adapting to changing circumstances without violating the
settlor’s core philanthropic vision.
Together, these doctrines create a harmonious system that balances individual autonomy in
property disposition with overarching principles of fairness, alienability, and the public interest.

X. Within the intricate framework of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, several equitable
doctrines operate to ensure justice, clarity, and the effective administration of property rights.
Among these, the Rule Against Perpetuity, the Doctrine of Election, and the Doctrine of Merger
serve as foundational pillars, while the related Doctrine of Cy-pres governs charitable trusts.


The Rule Against Perpetuity, encapsulated in Section 14, is a central pillar of property law
designed to prevent the tying up of property inalienably for an excessive period. It mandates
that no future interest in property is valid unless it must vest, if at all, within a life or lives in
being at the creation of the interest plus twenty-one years, excluding the period of gestation.
This rule strikes a crucial balance between allowing settlors to control the future devolution of
their assets and ensuring that property remains marketable and free from dead-hand control for
generations, thereby serving the public interest by facilitating its circulation in the economy.


The Doctrine of Election, detailed in Section 35, embodies the equitable maxim that one cannot
approbate and reprobate. It stipulates that if an instrument, such as a will or deed, purports to
transfer a property belonging to another person while also conferring a benefit on that same
person, the beneficiary must choose (elect) either to accept the benefit under the instrument,
thereby surrendering their own property, or to retain their own property, forfeiting the conferred
benefit. This doctrine ensures fairness by preventing a person from taking advantage of an
instrument while simultaneously disregarding its dispositive provisions.
Distinct from election, the Doctrine of Merger addresses the confluence of estates. It operates
automatically when a lesser estate and a greater estate in the same property unite in the same
person, in the same right, with no intermediate interest existing between them. For instance, if
a lessee acquires the freehold (ownership) of the leased property, the leasehold interest merges
into the freehold and extinguishes. The intent of the parties may sometimes prevent merger, but
the doctrine's primary purpose is to simplify the title by eliminating superfluous and coexisting
interests held by a single individual.
While the Doctrine of Cy-pres finds its statutory home in the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, it is
conceptually vital in property law concerning charitable trusts. It empowers the court, when
the specific purpose of a charitable trust becomes impossible or impracticable to fulfil, to direct
the trust property to be applied cy-pres (as near as possible) to the original general charitable
intent of the settlor. This prevents the failure of the trust and ensures that charitable resources
continue to serve the public good, adapting to changing circumstances without violating the
settlor’s core philanthropic vision.
Together, these doctrines create a harmonious system that balances individual autonomy in
property disposition with overarching principles of fairness, alienability, and the public interest.

XI. The discharge of a contract signifies the termination of the contractual relationship between
the parties, extinguishing their respective rights and obligations. The Indian Contract Act, 1872,
provides several distinct modes through which a contract can be legally discharged, moving
beyond mere completion.
The most ideal and frequent mode is discharge by performance (Section 37), where both parties
fulfil their promises precisely as per the terms. The contract is said to be discharged when the
obligations are executed, leaving no outstanding duties. Performance must be complete,
precise, and by the promisor or their authorised agent to be effective.
Parties may also mutually agree to end or modify their agreement. Discharge by agreement or
consent is facilitated under Sections 62 and 63. This encompasses novation, where an existing
contract is substituted with a new one involving either the same or new parties; rescission,
which involves the mutual abandonment of all contractual obligations; alteration, where one or
more terms are modified by mutual consent; and remission, where a promisee accepts a lesser
fulfilment than what was originally promised.
A contract may be discharged under the doctrine of frustration (Section 56), which deals with
subsequent impossibility or unlawfulness. If an event, unforeseen at the time of contracting and
not due to either party's fault, renders the performance impossible or radically different from
what was envisaged, the contract becomes void. Examples include destruction of the subject
matter, a change in law making performance illegal, or the death or incapacity of a person
crucial for performance. The core is the occurrence of a subsequent, unavoidable change in
circumstances.
Finally, discharge by breach (Section 39) occurs when one party fails to perform their
obligation. Breach can be actual, upon the failure to perform on the due date, or anticipatory,
where a party repudiates the contract before the performance is due. In an anticipatory breach,
the aggrieved party is immediately entitled to sue for damages without waiting for the actual
performance date. A breach, whether actual or anticipatory, does not automatically terminate
the contract; it gives the injured party the option to treat the contract as rescinded and claim
compensation, thereby discharging their own future obligations.
Thus, the Act provides a comprehensive framework, recognising that contractual bonds can
dissolve not only through successful execution but also through mutual accord, unforeseen
impossibility, or the failure of a party to uphold their promise.

       15. On June 10, before Bina could respond, a new law was passed making the

       key legal issue?

content.passageText:
XII. The constitutional mechanism for evolving India's official language policy is a carefully
crafted procedural compromise, established under Article 344 of the Constitution. This
provision mandates the President to constitute an Official Language Commission at the
expiration of ten years from the Constitution's commencement, and thereafter as deemed
necessary. However, the President's authority in appointing this Commission is not absolute. A
critical proviso to Clause (1) imposes a specific linguistic balance, requiring that the
Commission consist of members drawn in equal proportion from both the Hindi-speaking and
the non-Hindi-speaking states. This structural safeguard ensures regional and linguistic equity


in a body whose recommendations could significantly impact the Union's administrative
language.
The Commission's primary duty is to make recommendations to the President on the
progressive use of Hindi, the restrictions on English, and related matters. Its report, however,
does not take direct effect. It enters a unique deliberative phase where a Committee of
Parliament, comprising thirty members from the Lok Sabha and twenty from the Rajya Sabha,
scrutinizes it. The primary constitutional function of this Parliamentary Committee is to act as
a vital political filter, providing its own views and recommendations for the President's
consideration alongside the Commission's report. This creates a dialogic process between
expert recommendation and political consensus.
Following this, the President may issue a directive based on the Commission's
recommendations and the Committee's report. Crucially, Article 344(4) clarifies the nature of
this directive: it is expressly non-justiciable, and its implementation is left entirely to the
discretion of Parliament. This process inherently acknowledges a potential constitutional
tension. Recommendations to restrict English could impact civil servants from non-Hindi
regions, potentially engaging the fundamental right to equality of opportunity in matters of
public employment under Article 16, as language proficiency could become an unreasonable
barrier.
Historically, the first Official Language Commission (1955), chaired by B.G. Kher, played a
foundational role. While operating within its constitutional terms, it made an influential
recommendation that transcended its immediate mandate and became a cornerstone of national
policy: the adoption of a three-language formula in school education. This proposal aimed to
balance the promotion of Hindi, the continued use of English, and the study of a modern Indian
language, thereby embodying the pluralistic spirit of India's language policy framework.

A key constitutional tension exists between the mandate of the Official Language
    Commission under Article 344 and the fundamental rights of civil servants. If the
    Commission recommends restricting English for official purposes, which fundamental
    right of a civil servant, specifically protected under Article 16, might be invoked in a
    potential legal challenge?
options: Right to equality of opportunity in matters of public employment.
Right to freedom of speech and expression.

XII. The constitutional mechanism for evolving India's official language policy is a carefully
crafted procedural compromise, established under Article 344 of the Constitution. This
provision mandates the President to constitute an Official Language Commission at the
expiration of ten years from the Constitution's commencement, and thereafter as deemed
necessary. However, the President's authority in appointing this Commission is not absolute. A
critical proviso to Clause (1) imposes a specific linguistic balance, requiring that the
Commission consist of members drawn in equal proportion from both the Hindi-speaking and
the non-Hindi-speaking states. This structural safeguard ensures regional and linguistic equity


in a body whose recommendations could significantly impact the Union's administrative
language.
The Commission's primary duty is to make recommendations to the President on the
progressive use of Hindi, the restrictions on English, and related matters. Its report, however,
does not take direct effect. It enters a unique deliberative phase where a Committee of
Parliament, comprising thirty members from the Lok Sabha and twenty from the Rajya Sabha,
scrutinizes it. The primary constitutional function of this Parliamentary Committee is to act as
a vital political filter, providing its own views and recommendations for the President's
consideration alongside the Commission's report. This creates a dialogic process between
expert recommendation and political consensus.
Following this, the President may issue a directive based on the Commission's
recommendations and the Committee's report. Crucially, Article 344(4) clarifies the nature of
this directive: it is expressly non-justiciable, and its implementation is left entirely to the
discretion of Parliament. This process inherently acknowledges a potential constitutional
tension. Recommendations to restrict English could impact civil servants from non-Hindi
regions, potentially engaging the fundamental right to equality of opportunity in matters of
public employment under Article 16, as language proficiency could become an unreasonable
barrier.
Historically, the first Official Language Commission (1955), chaired by B.G. Kher, played a
foundational role. While operating within its constitutional terms, it made an influential
recommendation that transcended its immediate mandate and became a cornerstone of national
policy: the adoption of a three-language formula in school education. This proposal aimed to
balance the promotion of Hindi, the continued use of English, and the study of a modern Indian
language, thereby embodying the pluralistic spirit of India's language policy framework.

XIII. In its landmark ruling upholding Section 6A of the Citizenship Act, the Supreme Court's
majority opinion employed the Preambular value of "Fraternity" as a decisive constitutional
anchor. This rationale served to implicitly reject a significant alternative challenge: that the
provision was arbitrary for creating a special citizenship rule only for Assam, thereby violating
Article 14's guarantee of equality. The Court reasoned that the unique historical context of
migration into Assam, culminating in the Assam Accord, justified a differentiated legal
response to foster national unity and integration, thus satisfying the test of reasonable
classification under Article 14.
This conclusion was not unanimous. The dissenting opinion issued a profound caution, arguing
that accepting the petitioners’ claim of a demographic threat to cultural identity could establish
a dangerous precedent. This warning is best understood as an alert against legitimizing internal
discrimination based on origin, akin to creating "insiders" and "outsiders" within a state, which
could undermine the constitutional framework of a unified citizenship.
Acknowledging serious flaws in implementation, the majority issued a singular directive for
the Chief Justice of India to constitute a monitoring Bench. This extraordinary procedural
measure most closely aligns with the Court's strategic use of its power to exercise continuing
mandamus to ensure executive compliance with laws, a tool used to oversee complex, long-
term enforcement where governmental inaction has been chronic.
On the substantive question of cultural rights, the judgment clarified that the protection for any
section of citizens to conserve their distinct culture under Article 29(1) operates irrespective of
demographic change. This legal interpretation implies that this fundamental right is primarily
a guarantee against state action that actively destroys or prohibits the culture, not a shield
against demographic shifts resulting from lawful migration or political processes.
Ultimately, the Court emphasized that the petitioners failed to prove that Section 6A itself
compromised the Assamese people's cultural safeguards. This underscores a foundational
principle of constitutional litigation: a law is presumed valid, and the burden rests on the
challenger to demonstrate it is manifestly arbitrary or bears no reasonable nexus to a legitimate
state aim. The petitioners' inability to discharge this burden was central to the provision's
survival.

XIV. International law demonstrates its capacity for profound impact through specialized
treaties that address distinct global challenges. Two exemplary agreements, originating in
different decades and targeting vastly different threats, stand out for their successful,
convention-based approach: the Mine Ban Treaty and the Montreal Protocol.


The Mine Ban Treaty, formally known as the Ottawa Treaty, represents a landmark in
humanitarian disarmament law. It was driven by a coalition of states, civil society, and
international organizations horrified by the indiscriminate and lingering impact of anti-
personnel landmines on civilians, long after conflicts have ended. The treaty’s core obligations
are unequivocal: it prohibits the use, stockpiling, production, and transfer of anti-personnel
mines. It also mandates the clearance of mined areas and assistance for victims. By establishing
a clear norm against these weapons, the Ottawa Treaty has created a powerful stigma, leading
to a dramatic reduction in their use and the destruction of millions of stockpiled mines, saving
countless lives and limbs.
In the environmental sphere, the Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone
Layer is heralded as one of the most successful international treaties ever crafted. Confronted
with compelling scientific evidence that man-made chemicals were eroding the Earth’s
protective ozone layer, the international community acted decisively. The treaty is designed to
protect the ozone layer by phasing out the production and consumption of Ozone Depleting
Substances, such as chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and halons. Its innovative framework includes
binding phase-out schedules for developed and developing countries, a financial mechanism to
aid compliance, and a scientific assessment panel to guide its evolution. This adaptable,
science-based regime has led to the near-elimination of major ozone-depleting chemicals,
allowing the ozone layer to begin a slow recovery and providing a crucial model for multilateral
environmental cooperation.
Together, these treaties illustrate how focused legal instruments, built on scientific evidence or
humanitarian imperative and supported by robust implementation mechanisms, can deliver
tangible, life-preserving results for humanity and the planet.

content.passageText:
XVI. Imagine you are in charge of India's money. Your main job is to keep prices stable. Your
main tool is the repo rate, which is the interest rate at which you lend money to banks. When
you change this rate, it eventually changes the cost of every loan in the country, from big factory
loans to your family's car EMI. Recently, the RBI had a big meeting and kept the repo rate
unchanged at 5.25 per cent. On the surface, this looks like doing nothing. But in finance,
choosing to do nothing can be a powerful decision. Let us understand why.


The RBI watches two big things: inflation, which means how much prices rise, and growth,
which means how fast the economy expands. Ideally, inflation should be around 4 per cent.
Right now, inflation has fallen sharply to around 2-2.5 per cent, which is well below the target.
At the same time, the economy is still growing. So a simple textbook would say this is the
perfect moment to cut rates, because lower rates make loans cheaper and encourage spending.
So why did the RBI not cut?


The answer is that the RBI knows real life is more complicated. It looks at the story behind the
numbers. The first reason is that not all inflation drops are permanent. Inflation fell mainly
because food prices dropped. This is good news, but also tricky. In India, food prices go up and
down a lot. A drop might not last. If next year's monsoon is bad, food prices could shoot right
back up. If the RBI cuts rates now because of temporarily low food prices, it could backfire.
Cheaper loans would put more money in people's pockets. If food prices then rise again, people
will have more money to spend on expensive food, making inflation even worse. So the RBI
is waiting to see if this low inflation is here to stay or just a temporary visitor.


The second reason is that past decisions take time to work. Imagine watering a garden with a
long hose. When you turn the tap, water takes time to reach the plants. Similarly, when the RBI
cuts rates, it takes time for the effect to reach you through cheaper bank loans and lower EMIs.
The RBI has already cut rates significantly over the past year. That water is still flowing through
the system. If they cut again before the first cuts have fully worked, they might overwater the
garden and cause problems later. So when the RBI keeps rates on hold, it is not ignoring the
economy. It is being patient, watching carefully, and waiting to see what happens next.


[Extracted with revisions and edits from “RBI is buying time by not cutting the repo rate. Past
policy needs a breather to work”, ThePrint.]

content.passageText:
XVII. What makes human beings unique? Throughout history, we’ve given this quality many
names—the human spirit, the human condition, or the soul. Some have tried to explain it away,
arguing we’re just another animal. Others have called it divine, beyond explanation.


Today, this debate is heating up again. Artificial intelligence—specifically large language
models like ChatGPT—is challenging our assumptions about what makes us special. When
Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, tweeted “i am a stochastic parrot, and so r u,” he was responding
to linguist Emily Bender’s claim that these systems merely spit out predictable words without
real understanding. One side argues machines can never truly be like us. The other suggests the
differences aren’t so clear.


This isn’t the first time technology has sparked such conflict. During the Industrial Revolution,
society faced a similar divide. On one side were rationalists who saw human behaviour as
something to be measured, managed and optimised like a machine. On the other were
Romantics who defended subjective feeling, individual genius and the organic nature of human
life against the spread of mechanism.


Today, AI is reigniting this war across multiple fronts—science, art and politics. Can machines
truly be creative? Can they make ethical judgments? Or will there always remain something
essentially human that technology cannot capture?


To answer these questions, we need to look at three key areas: knowledge, beauty and morality.
In each domain, humans demonstrate capacities that may elude computation—wisdom in how
we apply knowledge, creativity in how we imagine new possibilities, and autonomy in how we
make moral choices.


The philosophers Immanuel Kant and G W F Hegel pointed to freedom as the core of human
uniqueness. But this freedom isn’t simple. It combines our ability to pursue truth, create beauty
and choose what’s right. Understanding these elements might help us not only appreciate our
own humanity but perhaps one day build machines that share in these pursuits.


Could we create artificial souls? The question is no longer just philosophical. It’s becoming
urgent.


[Extracted with revisions and edits from “Geist in the machine”, aeon.]

content.passageText:
I. For some wealthy Ferrari NV customers the biggest thrill of 2025 wasn’t the launch of
some flashy new technology or supercar model, but rather the prancing horse’s reversion to
using simple mechanical buttons to control aspects of the vehicle. When buyers were told the
Italian carmaker is moving away from finicky touch-sensitive controls on the steering wheel
and going back to buttons there was “big, big applause,” Chief Executive Officer Benedetto
Vigna told Bloomberg TV last week, emphasizing that the company will henceforth use
“digital where it’s needed, and physical where it’s needed.”


Ferrari’s epiphany is the latest example of a manufacturer reappraising the minimalist and
futuristic design trends that have transformed the automobile in recent years — not always
for the better. With Tesla Inc. and software-loving Chinese rivals leading the way, cars have
started to feel like battery-powered cell phones on wheels. That’s led to impressive
innovations such as advanced safety features and automated driving, but also a tendency to
reengineer stuff that worked fine already, including door handles, glove box latches and
indicator stalks.

Perhaps this urge to reinvent is a byproduct of how other aspects of car design have become
so bland. But in this push for smooth interior perfection, simple tasks like adjusting the air
conditioning are often less intuitive. Fiddling with the right settings on the ubiquitous flat-
screen is potentially dangerous when on the road. What seems fun to a twentysomething
automotive software engineer, or to China’s young tech-savvy consumers, might feel
annoyingly complicated to 50-something Western buyers. Automakers should adapt for
different markets.

Until vehicles are fully driverless, manufacturers need to strike a balance between aesthetics,
efficiency and digitalization on one hand, and sticking with physical controls where needed


for safety and ease of use. Doing everything with a touchscreen or reinventing the humble
door handle is asking for trouble.

SOURCE:https://www.bloomberg.com/opinion/articles/2025-10-24/ferrari-s-crowd-pleasing-
retro-refit-is-pushing-all-the-right-buttons

content.passageText:
I. For some wealthy Ferrari NV customers the biggest thrill of 2025 wasn’t the launch of
some flashy new technology or supercar model, but rather the prancing horse’s reversion to
using simple mechanical buttons to control aspects of the vehicle. When buyers were told the
Italian carmaker is moving away from finicky touch-sensitive controls on the steering wheel
and going back to buttons there was “big, big applause,” Chief Executive Officer Benedetto
Vigna told Bloomberg TV last week, emphasizing that the company will henceforth use
“digital where it’s needed, and physical where it’s needed.”


Ferrari’s epiphany is the latest example of a manufacturer reappraising the minimalist and
futuristic design trends that have transformed the automobile in recent years — not always
for the better. With Tesla Inc. and software-loving Chinese rivals leading the way, cars have
started to feel like battery-powered cell phones on wheels. That’s led to impressive
innovations such as advanced safety features and automated driving, but also a tendency to
reengineer stuff that worked fine already, including door handles, glove box latches and
indicator stalks.

Perhaps this urge to reinvent is a byproduct of how other aspects of car design have become
so bland. But in this push for smooth interior perfection, simple tasks like adjusting the air
conditioning are often less intuitive. Fiddling with the right settings on the ubiquitous flat-
screen is potentially dangerous when on the road. What seems fun to a twentysomething
automotive software engineer, or to China’s young tech-savvy consumers, might feel
annoyingly complicated to 50-something Western buyers. Automakers should adapt for
different markets.

Until vehicles are fully driverless, manufacturers need to strike a balance between aesthetics,
efficiency and digitalization on one hand, and sticking with physical controls where needed


for safety and ease of use. Doing everything with a touchscreen or reinventing the humble
door handle is asking for trouble.

content.passageText:
II. Knowing that Mrs. Mallard was afflicted with a heart trouble, great care was taken to break
to her as gently as possible the news of her husband's death.


It was her sister Josephine who told her, in broken sentences, veiled hints that revealed in half
concealing. Her husband's friend Richards was there, too, near her. It was he who had been in
the newspaper office when intelligence of the railroad disaster was received, with Brently
Mallard's name leading the list of "killed." He had only taken the time to assure himself of its
truth by a second telegram, and had hastened to forestall any less careful, less tender friend in
bearing the sad message.

She did not hear the story as many women have heard the same, with a paralyzed inability to
accept its significance. She wept at once, with sudden, wild abandonment, in her sister's arms.
When the storm of grief had spent itself she went away to her room alone. She would have no
one follow her. There stood, facing the open window, a comfortable, roomy armchair. Into this
she sank, pressed down by a physical exhaustion that haunted her body and seemed to reach
into her soul.

She could see in the open square before her house the tops of trees that were all aquiver with
the new spring life. The delicious breath of rain was in the air. In the street below a peddler was
crying his wares. The notes of a distant song which someone was singing reached her faintly,
and countless sparrows were twittering in the eaves. There were patches of blue sky showing
here and there through the clouds that had met and piled one above the other in the west facing
her window.

She sat with her head thrown back upon the cushion of the chair, quite motionless, except when
a sob came up into her throat and shook her, as a child who has cried itself to sleep continues
to sob in its dreams. She was young, with a fair, calm face, whose lines bespoke repression and
even a certain strength. But now there was a dull stare in her eyes, whose gaze was fixed away
off yonder on one of those patches of blue sky. It was not a glance of reflection, but rather
indicated a suspension of intelligent thought.

There was something coming to her and she was waiting for it, fearfully. What was it? She did
not know; it was too subtle and elusive to name. But she felt it, creeping out of the sky, reaching
toward her through the sounds, the scents, the color that filled the air.

III. Saudi Arabia’s reform of its sponsorship programme for overseas workers is seen as a
precursor to the kingdom opening up to foreign investment as it diversifies its economy away
from oil. But alterations to the kafala system are partial, with sponsorship still mandated to
secure entry, although exit and job changes have been freed for a wide category of expatriate
labour. The segment most vulnerable to exploitation, domestic help, is not covered by the new
rules. Saudi Arabia thus swells the ranks of members of Gulf Coordination Council (GCC) that
are reforming their regimes for foreign workers under pressure by economic forces to seek a
future beyond natural resources. The measures remain considerably below internationally
accepted norms on labour mobility.


Yet labour reforms are vital for Saudi Arabia. Over 40% of workers are foreigners, the majority
of them from South Asia, including India. The country has accelerated its infrastructure build-
up and is dependent on labour-intensive construction during the transition. As a key supplier
of migrant workers and a big buyer of oil, India should leverage itself to play a bigger role in
Saudi Arabia’s transformation. India is also building railways, airports and ports. The
experience will come in handy for similar business in the Persian Gulf.

Relaxations to the kafala system are part of Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030, which coincides with
commitments by some of the world’s largest economies to transition to RE. Oil-producing
nations will also need to develop their transition strategies. Here, too, India could play a
constructive role in the Gulf. So long as India remains among the fastest-growing major
economies, it will improve its capacity to engage with countries like Saudi Arabia in emerging
sectors. Negotiations are on for an FTA with GCC, and India has been fairly spiffy in signing
bilateral agreements with some of its members. Saudi Arabia would be the biggest catch in this
haul.

our indigenous breeds. Before colonial rule, Indian dog breeds were valued at home. Their
speed, strength and loyalty also meant that they were sought after abroad. Ancient Greek,
Roman and Chinese records indicate they were recognised as distinct and superior. But British
rule saw a deep reversal of such ideas. As their kennel culture and their standards of ‘breeding’
and ‘purity’ took root, Indian breeds came to be seen as inferior, mongrels, ‘street dogs’, even


‘pariah dogs’. A counter-reversal is being attempted at the institutional level and this is very
much the right thing to do.

from Thar desert to Tawang. Indie breeds, it is now beginning to be seen, are better adapted to
Indian conditions. This shift wouldn’t have taken so long if our colonial inheritance hadn’t been
topped up with long, postcolonial inertia. During decades of a closed economy, the imported-
is-good and local-is-bad binary stultified. And this socialist overhang continued even
afterwards. Pugs, Shihtzus, Rottweilers…have carried status like designer bags and cars.

V. On the face of it, a ruling by the Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (CDRC) in
Ahmedabad that fined a tailor for not delivering an order on time and according to customer
specifications sounds like a piffle. But this 'small' case study should be viewed seriously. It
reflects a larger story that has gnawed away at the otherwise much-feted Indian services
industry: consumer apathy in the face of subpar services.

The services sector, a cornerstone of India's economic growth, is paradoxically plagued by a
culture of casual neglect toward consumer grievances. From erratic broadband connections and
opaque billing in hospitals to airline grievances and cab hailing/delivery app malpractices, the
average Indian consumer is expected to endure incompetence with stoic patience and treat it as
'par for the course'. CDRC, along with consumer protection laws, must be treated not as
bureaucratic ornaments but as vital instruments of accountability.

CDRC is not a complaint box. It's a quasi-judicial body empowered to enforce consumer rights.
Yet, its potential is squandered when citizens treat it as a last resort, and companies and
businesses dismiss it as toothless. The truth is, every unresolved complaint is a missed
opportunity to raise service standards. When grievances are formally registered and pursued,
they create pressure points that force businesses to improve, and compete on quality - not just
price. Consumer Protection Act of 2019 introduced e-filing, product liability and stricter
penalties. But laws are only as strong as the public's will to invoke them. If consumers remain
passive, and if businesses continue to view redressal as optional, the services sector - especially
as India tries to plug into global supply chains - will remain afloat in mediocrity.

Supreme Court and continued to place excessive procedural burdens on individuals seeking legal
recognition of gender identity. Protests were organised across several cities, with activists demanding

frameworks and lived realities of transgender communities in India. While the government defended
the amendments as administrative improvements, opponents contended that the reforms must align
more closely with constitutional guarantees of dignity, equality, and personal autonomy. The debate
reflects the broader challenge of translating progressive judicial pronouncements into effective statutory
protections.

Rights) Act, ______-, triggering significant debate among activists, legal scholars, and policymakers.

stronger protections against discrimination, clearer reservation policies, and greater recognition of self-
identification rights. The controversy also revived discussions around the gap between legislative
frameworks and lived realities of transgender communities in India. While the government defended
the amendments as administrative improvements, opponents contended that the reforms must align
more closely with constitutional guarantees of dignity, equality, and personal autonomy. The debate
reflects the broader challenge of translating progressive judicial pronouncements into effective statutory
protections.

VIII. The consolidation of British power in India can be traced back to two decisive military
engagements in the 18th century—the Battle of Plassey and the Battle of Buxar. These battles marked
a turning point in the transformation of the British East India Company from a trading enterprise into a
territorial power.


The Battle of Plassey was fought between the Company, led by Robert Clive, and the Nawab of Bengal,
Siraj-ud-Daulah. The victory was facilitated by internal betrayal, particularly by Mir Jafar, which
enabled the Company to gain political influence in Bengal. However, it was the Battle of Buxar that
firmly established British authority, as the Company defeated a combined force of Indian rulers
including the Mughal Emperor and the Nawab of Awadh.


Following Buxar, the Company secured the Diwani rights of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa, granting it
control over revenue collection. These developments laid the foundation of British colonial rule in India.


Source: The Hindu Archives

Legal Reasoning


IX. The legal institution of reservations is a critical mechanism in treaty law, balancing state
sovereignty with the integrity of multilateral conventions. Under Article 2(1)(d) of the Vienna
Convention on the Law of Treaties (VCLT), a reservation is defined as a unilateral statement
made by a State when consenting to a treaty, whereby it purports to exclude or modify the legal
effect of certain provisions in their application to that State.

The governing legal regime represents a significant shift from the traditional unanimity rule,
which required acceptance by all contracting states. The VCLT introduced a more flexible
system to encourage widespread treaty participation. Under Article 19, a State may formulate
a reservation unless: it is prohibited by the treaty; the treaty permits only specified reservations;
or the reservation is incompatible with the treaty's object and purpose. This "object and
purpose" test serves as the fundamental limit on the reservation power.

The legal effects of reservations and objections are detailed in Articles 20 and 21. When a
reservation is accepted by another contracting state, either expressly or tacitly, the reserving
state becomes a party in relation to that accepting state, with treaty provisions modified to the
extent of the reservation. Conversely, an objection does not necessarily preclude treaty relations
unless a contrary intention is definitely expressed. If the treaty enters into force, the provisions
to which the reservation relates do not apply as between the two states to the extent of the
reservation.

Beyond reservations, the temporal operation of treaties is governed by distinct rules. Under
Article 24, a treaty enters into force as it may provide or as negotiating states agree. Where no
provision exists, it enters force once consent is established for all negotiating states. Pursuant
to Article 28, treaties are non-retroactive unless a different intention appears. Finally, Article
25 allows for provisional application of a treaty pending its entry into force, enabling states to
implement obligations immediately without awaiting formal ratification procedures.

content.passageText:
X. Under the Parsi Marriage and Divorce Act, 1936, the institution of marriage is afforded a
distinct legal identity, meticulously codified to preserve the community's religious ethos while
aligning with modern statutory requirements. The solemnization of a Parsi marriage is
inherently religious, legally recognized only when performed through the Ashivand ceremony.
This ceremony, officiated by a Parsi priest (Dastur or Mobed) before a sacred fire, involves the
ritualistic tying of a thread around the couple and the exchange of vows, binding them
according to Zoroastrian law.

For a marriage to be deemed valid under the Act, stringent conditions must be met. The parties
must not be related to each other within the prohibited degrees of consanguinity (blood relation)
or affinity (relation by marriage), as defined by the Act. Furthermore, the marriage must be free
from bigamy, requiring both parties to be unmarried and capable of giving valid consent. A
critical prerequisite for validity is the execution of the "Wedding Certificate," known as the
Jotan or Lagna-nam. This written contract, signed by the contracting parties, the officiating
priest, and two witnesses, serves as the foundational document of the union and must be
produced before the Registrar.

The legal recognition of the marriage is perfected through mandatory registration. Following
the ceremony, the Jotan must be forwarded to the Registrar of Marriages appointed under the
Act within fourteen days. The Registrar then enters the particulars into the official Marriage
Register. This registration is not merely procedural but acts as conclusive evidence of the
marriage having been duly solemnized, providing public notice and legal certainty regarding
the status of the parties.

Finally, a unique feature of Parsi matrimonial jurisprudence is the constitution of the Parsi
Matrimonial Courts. These are special courts with exclusive jurisdiction to adjudicate
matrimonial disputes. Their composition is unique: they consist of a High Court judge (or a
District Judge in certain cases) sitting alongside a board of five Parsi lay members, known as
Delegates. The law distinctly divides the functions of these two components. The Delegates,
being peers from the community, are the sole judges of questions of fact—such as determining
whether alleged cruelty or desertion has occurred. Once the facts are established by the
Delegates, the judge applies the relevant legal principles and passes the final decree. This
structure ensures that community standards inform the factual assessment while the rule of law
governs the ultimate outcome. Collectively, these provisions under the Act create a


comprehensive framework that safeguards the sanctity of Parsi marriage through religious
adherence, contractual certainty, public registration, and specialized adjudication.

XI. The Regulating Act of 1773 represents a pivotal moment in the constitutional history of
British India, marking the beginning of parliamentary oversight over the East India Company.
Prior to its enactment, the Company had operated largely as an autonomous commercial entity,
wielding immense power over vast territories with minimal external supervision. The British
government, prompted by reports of administrative corruption, financial mismanagement, and
the Company's desperate appeal for a loan to avert bankruptcy, resolved to intervene directly
in Indian affairs.

The legislation fundamentally restructured the administrative framework of the Company's
possessions. It recognized that the Company had transformed from a trading corporation into
a ruling power following its victories at Plassey and Buxar. The Act sought to introduce
principles of accountability and centralized direction, acknowledging that scattered British
settlements required coordinated governance. This recognition stemmed from the
understanding that independent action by individual presidencies could jeopardize British
interests and lead to conflicts with Indian powers.

In its structural design, the Act created a complex system of checks and balances reflecting
contemporary British constitutional thinking. It established mechanisms for oversight both in
India and in London, attempting to balance decisive executive action with safeguards against
arbitrary power. This dual concern shaped the institutional arrangements prescribed for
governing British territories.

The judicial provisions represented another significant departure from previous practice. By
providing for a crown court in Indian territory, Parliament introduced direct royal authority into
a domain previously governed exclusively by Company regulations. This created a dual judicial
system that would generate considerable jurisdictional conflict as the new court and existing
Company courts struggled to define their respective spheres.

Financial transparency formed a key legislative objective. The Act required detailed reporting
of revenues and expenditures, seeking to introduce regular accounting practices where none


had previously existed. This reflected Parliament's desire to understand the Company's true
financial position and ensure proper utilization of Indian revenues. The disclosure requirement
extended to political and military affairs, establishing a precedent for ongoing parliamentary
scrutiny.

The Act's approach to corruption reflected contemporary moral concerns about Company
servants in India. Reports of individuals acquiring immense fortunes through exploitative
means had created political pressure for reform. The legislation therefore addressed personal

XI. The Regulating Act of 1773 represents a pivotal moment in the constitutional history of
British India, marking the beginning of parliamentary oversight over the East India Company.
Prior to its enactment, the Company had operated largely as an autonomous commercial entity,
wielding immense power over vast territories with minimal external supervision. The British
government, prompted by reports of administrative corruption, financial mismanagement, and
the Company's desperate appeal for a loan to avert bankruptcy, resolved to intervene directly
in Indian affairs.

The legislation fundamentally restructured the administrative framework of the Company's
possessions. It recognized that the Company had transformed from a trading corporation into
a ruling power following its victories at Plassey and Buxar. The Act sought to introduce
principles of accountability and centralized direction, acknowledging that scattered British
settlements required coordinated governance. This recognition stemmed from the
understanding that independent action by individual presidencies could jeopardize British
interests and lead to conflicts with Indian powers.

In its structural design, the Act created a complex system of checks and balances reflecting
contemporary British constitutional thinking. It established mechanisms for oversight both in
India and in London, attempting to balance decisive executive action with safeguards against
arbitrary power. This dual concern shaped the institutional arrangements prescribed for
governing British territories.

The judicial provisions represented another significant departure from previous practice. By
providing for a crown court in Indian territory, Parliament introduced direct royal authority into
a domain previously governed exclusively by Company regulations. This created a dual judicial
system that would generate considerable jurisdictional conflict as the new court and existing
Company courts struggled to define their respective spheres.

Financial transparency formed a key legislative objective. The Act required detailed reporting
of revenues and expenditures, seeking to introduce regular accounting practices where none


had previously existed. This reflected Parliament's desire to understand the Company's true
financial position and ensure proper utilization of Indian revenues. The disclosure requirement
extended to political and military affairs, establishing a precedent for ongoing parliamentary
scrutiny.

The Act's approach to corruption reflected contemporary moral concerns about Company
servants in India. Reports of individuals acquiring immense fortunes through exploitative
means had created political pressure for reform. The legislation therefore addressed personal
conduct, seeking to establish behavioral standards that would restore public confidence in
British administration.

content.passageText:
XII. The Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) stands as the preeminent apex statutory body
in India, tasked with the vital role of combating corruption and promoting integrity within the
vast machinery of the Central Government. Its establishment was not a spontaneous event but
the result of a considered recommendation by the Santhanam Committee on Prevention of
Corruption, which submitted its report between 1962 and 1964. Acting on this advice, the
government constituted the CVC in 1964, though it initially functioned as a non-statutory body.
It was only in 2003 that its status was formalized and fortified through the enactment of the
Central Vigilance Commission Act, 2003, which governs its composition, powers, and
functions to this day.

Regarding its structural composition, the CVC is designed as a multi-member body to ensure
collective wisdom and balanced decision-making. The Commission is mandated to consist of
one Central Vigilance Commissioner, who serves as its Chairperson, and up to two Vigilance
Commissioners. This structure ensures a plurality of perspectives in its oversight and advisory
roles. The process of appointing these Commissioners is deliberately insulated from purely
executive control to preserve their impartiality. The President of India makes the appointment,
but only on the direct recommendation of a high-powered committee. This committee is
specifically constituted with the Prime Minister as its Chair, the Union Home Minister as a


member, and the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha as the third member, ensuring a
balance between the ruling party and the opposition in this crucial decision.

Once appointed, a Vigilance Commissioner holds office for a fixed term to safeguard against
arbitrary removal. The tenure is prescribed as four years from the date of assuming office, or
until the Commissioner attains the age of sixty-five years, whichever occurs earlier. This
provides a degree of certainty and stability to the leadership of the Commission. Furthermore,
the CVC's operational independence from the executive is reinforced through several critical
provisions. Its expenses, including the salaries and allowances of its members, are charged on
the Consolidated Fund of India. This constitutional mechanism means these expenditures are
not subject to the annual vote of Parliament, thereby shielding the Commission's budget from
potential political pressure or retaliation for its vigilance activities. This financial autonomy,
combined with its secure tenure, allows the CVC to function as a robust and independent
watchdog against corruption.

XIII. The ultimate purpose of a tort claim is to secure a remedy for the harm suffered. The law
provides several distinct forms of relief designed to compensate the victim, punish the
wrongdoer, and prevent future misconduct. The most common remedy is an award of damages,
which is a sum of money paid by the defendant to the successful plaintiff.

The primary category is Compensatory Damages, which aim to make the plaintiff "whole"
again by restoring them to the position they would have been in had the tort not occurred. This
category is divided into two sub-types. Special Damages cover quantifiable economic losses


with specific monetary value. These are tangible and calculable, including past and future
medical expenses, lost wages and earning capacity, and the cost of repairing or replacing
damaged property. In contrast, General Damages compensate for non-economic, subjective
losses that are more difficult to calculate. These address the intangible consequences of an
injury, such as physical pain and suffering, emotional distress, mental anguish, and loss of
enjoyment of life. For instance, a plaintiff might recover special damages for hospital bills
while also receiving general damages for ongoing physical trauma.

Beyond compensation, tort law recognizes the need for punishment through Punitive or
Exemplary Damages. Unlike compensatory damages, which benefit the plaintiff, punitive
damages are awarded to punish the defendant for particularly reprehensible conduct. This
remedy is reserved for cases involving malice, fraud, or a conscious and reckless disregard for
the safety of others. By imposing a financial penalty far exceeding the actual harm caused,
punitive damages serve a vital public policy function: they deter the specific defendant and
others from engaging in similar outrageous behavior in the future.

Finally, not all remedies are monetary. In many situations, particularly those involving ongoing
harm, money alone is insufficient. Injunctive Relief is an equitable remedy in the form of a
court order that compels a party to do or refrain from doing a specific act. This is most common
in nuisance cases, where a court might issue an injunction to stop a factory from emitting
noxious fumes or to order a neighbor to remove an unlawful structure. The threat of contempt
of court provides a powerful mechanism to prevent irreparable harm that money damages could
not adequately address. Together, these remedies form a comprehensive system to address the
multifaceted nature of civil wrongs.

XIII. The ultimate purpose of a tort claim is to secure a remedy for the harm suffered. The law
provides several distinct forms of relief designed to compensate the victim, punish the
wrongdoer, and prevent future misconduct. The most common remedy is an award of damages,
which is a sum of money paid by the defendant to the successful plaintiff.

The primary category is Compensatory Damages, which aim to make the plaintiff "whole"
again by restoring them to the position they would have been in had the tort not occurred. This
category is divided into two sub-types. Special Damages cover quantifiable economic losses


with specific monetary value. These are tangible and calculable, including past and future
medical expenses, lost wages and earning capacity, and the cost of repairing or replacing
damaged property. In contrast, General Damages compensate for non-economic, subjective
losses that are more difficult to calculate. These address the intangible consequences of an
injury, such as physical pain and suffering, emotional distress, mental anguish, and loss of
enjoyment of life. For instance, a plaintiff might recover special damages for hospital bills
while also receiving general damages for ongoing physical trauma.

Beyond compensation, tort law recognizes the need for punishment through Punitive or
Exemplary Damages. Unlike compensatory damages, which benefit the plaintiff, punitive
damages are awarded to punish the defendant for particularly reprehensible conduct. This
remedy is reserved for cases involving malice, fraud, or a conscious and reckless disregard for
the safety of others. By imposing a financial penalty far exceeding the actual harm caused,
punitive damages serve a vital public policy function: they deter the specific defendant and
others from engaging in similar outrageous behavior in the future.

Finally, not all remedies are monetary. In many situations, particularly those involving ongoing
harm, money alone is insufficient. Injunctive Relief is an equitable remedy in the form of a
court order that compels a party to do or refrain from doing a specific act. This is most common
in nuisance cases, where a court might issue an injunction to stop a factory from emitting
noxious fumes or to order a neighbor to remove an unlawful structure. The threat of contempt
of court provides a powerful mechanism to prevent irreparable harm that money damages could
not adequately address. Together, these remedies form a comprehensive system to address the
multifaceted nature of civil wrongs.

XIV. The legal framework governing the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is primarily rooted in
two pivotal legislations: the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, and the Banking Regulation Act,
1949. The RBI was established under the provisions of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934,
which serves as the foundational statute defining its constitution and core functions. This Act,
which came into force on April 1, 1935, originally established the bank as a private entity
before its nationalization in 1949. Its Preamble outlines the bank's statutory raison d'être,
declaring its objective to be the regulation of the issue of bank notes and the keeping of reserves
with a view to securing monetary stability in India. This explicitly confirms that a primary
statutory function is to regulate note issue and manage reserves for monetary stability, not to
generate profit or engage in retail banking.

A cornerstone of the RBI's authority is derived from Section 22 of the RBI Act, which grants
it the sole right to issue banknotes in India. This exclusive privilege is legally termed the
Monopoly of Note Issue, a function that centralizes currency management and ensures
uniformity and public confidence. Complementing this power, Section 24 of the same Act
dictates the denominations of banknotes the RBI is authorized to print. The statute prescribes
that the minimum denomination shall be one rupee and the maximum denomination shall be
ten thousand rupees.

While the RBI Act establishes the central bank, the regulation of commercial banks falls under
the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. This Act empowers the RBI to perform its role as the
primary regulator of the banking sector. It is under this Act that the RBI derives its authority
for crucial functions such as granting licenses for new banks, prescribing capital requirements,


and overseeing the management of banking companies. Furthermore, specific powers like the
ability to issue directions to banks regarding their auditing practices are found within this Act,
notably in Section 35A. This section grants the RBI the power to issue directives in the public
interest or to prevent the affairs of any banking company from being conducted in a manner
detrimental to the interests of the depositors.

Logical Reasoning


XV. Keir Starmer is now the only person to have lost more comms chiefs than Meghan and
Harry. After yet another day of drama, we kept hearing that the prime minister would be
pressing the reset button. Not again! Starmer’s reset button is like the OK button on your TV
remote – worn blank through overuse. He has pressed that thing more often than you’ve decided
another 44 minutes of a crap thriller is somehow less of an effort than getting yourself to bed.
Anyway, next episode in five, four, three …

Fine. One more.

The inciting incident for yesterday’s deranged chapter was another comms chief leaving,
followed by an objectively hilarious call for Starmer’s resignation by the Scottish Labour
leader, Anas Sarwar, that accidentally forced Labour’s big guns to swing publicly behind
Starmer. That said, you couldn’t claim the cabinet came off as one big happy family, with a
minister briefing darkly: “We’ve all been made to tweet.” Buck up, Cruz. Think of Sarwar as
the Labour family’s Brooklyn Beckham, the latter having notably observed last month that
“Family ‘love’ is decided by how much you post on social media”.

Anyway, having seen off Sarwar’s desiccated power move, Starmer supposedly crushed it at
Monday evening’s gathering of the parliamentary Labour party. Entering the meeting room,


the PM is reported to have got a standing ovation that lasted 37 seconds. But don’t set too much
store by a standing ovation. At the Cannes film festival, you can get double that even for a
documentary claiming that every single Cannes film festival attender is a necrophiliac
bestialist. A fired-up Starmer apparently told his parliamentary colleagues: “I have won every
fight I’ve ever been in.” The prime minister is now seeking a match-up with either Jake Paul
or Tommy Fury.

He can butch it up all he likes, but the Peter Mandelson revelations have exposed Starmer as
an alleged fallen nice guy and dubious ally to women. He’s kind of the Justin Baldoni of
Westminster. Who’s the Blake Lively in all this? I desperately want to quit this analogy but find
it impossible when Wes Streeting keeps claiming that he is being covertly briefed against by
Starmer’s team. If these dark arts start to impact unit sales of Wes’s affordable haircare line it
may be time to go nuclear.

[Extracted with revisions and edits from “It’s nothing short of TV gold: mix horror with wild
comedy and call it Starmer’s last stand”, The Guardian.]
